title: Spain’s SETT Drives $521 Million Investment Push to Build Global Audiovisual Players
full_text: Sep 19, 2026 2:55am PT Spain’s SETT Drives $521 Million Investment Push to Build Global Audiovisual Players Spearheading the Spain Audiovisual Hub Phase 2, SETT, a state-backed venture capital fund, represents new opportunities for Spain’s film and TV industries By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest Writer-Star Berto Romero, Director Javier Ruiz Caldera Unpack San Sebastian Buzz Title ‘5 More Minutes’: ‘Characters and Audience Should Feel Every Second’s Weight’ 4 hours ago TV Operators Power Spain’s Global Breakout as the San Sebastian Film Festival Readies Launch: ‘Spanish Cinema Has Never Been So Powerful’ 19 hours ago Juan Andrés García Ropero ‘Bropi,’ the New Director of Contents of Movistar Plus, on Its San Sebastián Titles, Strategy 19 hours ago See All 'People of the Book,' the first film from Good Films Studios Spain Courtesy of GFSS No Spanish industry initiative is likely to drive more conversation at this year’s San Sebastián Festival than the latest moves by the Spanish Society for Technological Transformation ( SETT ). Over the past 12 months, state-backed venture capital fund SETT, the investment driver of the Spain Audiovisual Hub , has plowed €215.6 million ($252.3 million) into Spain’s film, TV, video game and new technology sectors, sparking matching private-sector investment of a further €230 million ($269.1 million), says María González Veracruz, Spain’s secretary of state for digitalization and artificial intelligence. That’s around four times the average budget of Spain’s core subsidy fund at the country‘s ICAA Film Board. Popular on Variety In other ways, SETT, which is part of Spain’s Ministry for Digital Transformation, also harbors a revolution. Since the 1940s, Spanish governments have offered subsidy grants and loans for individual films, and from around 2015, tax breaks on shoots in Spain. In contrast, SETT invests up to 10 years in companies with a portfolio of productions, requiring co-investment from private-sector partners, and looking to give them an edge in the international market. It also backs private-sector investment vehicles. “We are moving from an era of encouraging an ecosystem to consolidating a truly international audiovisual industry,” says González Veracruz. Eleven of 15 SETT investments have been made public to date, with beneficiaries including animation sector leaders ( Anima Kitchent , Amuse Animation, Planeta Junior), new Spain-based production companies ( Good Films Studios Spain , Ítaca Films Madrid, Moonlighting Studios Spain), post-production facilities ( Lazona Audiovisual Hub, the Refinery) and a full chain-of-value production-distribution player (Impulse Studio). Also underscoring the range of SETT’s portfolio, risk capital fund partners include Aurora Media Inversiones, led by the Secuoya Content Group, Culture CAP7, which targets small- to medium-sized enterprises, and elevated genre specialist Moby Dick Film Capital. Serving as a “public catalyst for growth, employment, innovation and talent, which are all core elements of the audiovisual sector,” SETT brings to the table the weight and power of the Spanish government and European Union backing, says SETT director general Javier Ponce. With the Spain Audiovisual Hub a key element of Spain’s post-COVID Recovery Plan, SETT’s funding is financed through the European Union’s Next Generation funds, Ponce notes. Its model has been built on three pillars, adds SETT audiovisual director María Coronado: “First, it adopts an industrywide approach, rather than a project-based one, addressing the entire audiovisual business ecosystem. Second, its investment facilities are directed at the equity capital of companies or regulated investment vehicles. Third, it promotes public-private partnership instruments in the medium to long term.” Companies must represent a “worthwhile business opportunity,” she adds. As global markets have contracted to some 75% of peak TV, according to Ampere Analysis, however, where are these opportunities? The key to SETT is its specific operations. SETT has taken a 46% stake for €19.8 million ($22.6 million), for instance, in Good Films Studios Spain, set up at Spain’s Ciudad de la Luz, one of Spain’s biggest studio complexes. It aims to make competitive English-language movies, budgeted at €15 million-€25 million ($17.5 million-$29.3 million) “with stars of international theatrical market value,” says GFSS head Miriam Segal, producer of “Good,” with Viggo Mortensen and “The Infiltrator,” starring Bryan Cranston. Attracting such stars, however, is ever more difficult, she adds. “So it makes making independent films at this level very, very hard. So to have a government body like SETT and hopefully new producer-driven tax incentives, it’s like I died and went to heaven,” says Segal. “In a world that’s receding, to have a country with the vision to support filmmakers, independence, training and creation of an industry is very exciting.” Established in Madrid by Roberto Butragueño and Andrés Sánchez Pajares and co-owned by SETT, Impulse Studio offers everything, from upstream development to financing, production, post-production, international sales and distribution. “When we talk with potential partners on projects or potential investors, we have the stamp of security of government backing,” says Sánchez Pajares. With SETT’s support, we can bring “hard equity” to the table, retaining part of the IP, “and offer all services at any phase of a project,” says Sánchez, Impulse Studio CEO. “I think that will allow us to sit at tables where we were not able to talk to date.” Further growth opportunities turn on scaling up animation projects aimed at the preschool audience. In another move, investing €9.2 million ($10.7 million) and partnering with Planeta Junior and Amuse Animation, SETT co-bought select distribution rights to hit preschool toon series “Milo,” sold to 186 territories, across multiple formats. “‘Milo’ represents a strategic opportunity in the field of technology development, particularly in software, video games and mobile applications,” says Coronado. “Spain has already established itself as one of Europe’s most attractive production hubs, thanks to its combination of creative talent, production incentives, and infrastructure,” says Maria Rua Aguete at London-based consultancy Omdia. “The next logical step is for Spain to transition from being a production destination to building globally competitive Spanish companies that own and export intellectual property.” EU Next Generation funds ran out on Aug. 30. SETT doesn’t aim to stop here, however. “The audiovisual sector will remain one of SETT’s strategic areas of activity and will continue under new fund, España Crece. We have begun discussions with [Spanish state bank] ICO to define the procedures and framework for collaboration between the two institutions, ensuring the continuation of co-investment in strategic technologies and sectors,” says Ponce. A Drill Down on Further SETT Investments “ The goal of the Hub’s second phase is clear: that Spain continues to be not only a great place to film, but also a great place to create, produce, finance, and export content, technology, and intellectual property to the world,” says González Veracruz. She adds: “ It’s a portfolio that reflects an industrial, technological, domestic and international view of Spanish audiovisual production.” A breakdown of announced SETT investments: *South Africa’s Known Associates Group and SETT have invested a joint €25 million ($29 million) to launch Moonlighting Studios Spain, a Madrid-based production company, and post-pro The Refinery, with facilities in the Basque Country and the Canary Islands. *Alongside DNEG , “The Odyssey’s” sole VFX partner, SETT has taken €24.9 million ($29.1 million) equity in the Canary Islands’ Anima Kitchen, behind pre-school animation series hits “Cleo & Cuquín.” Anima Kitchent is renowned for leveraging YouTube, where it has over 67 million subscribers, in order to launch and consolidate IPs. “The real edge is the combination: strong IP and production values paired with data analysis that tracks audience trends in real time. Producing quickly and at high quality is precisely what makes that IPs travel into new markets,” comments Pablo Hernández, executive president of the Canary Islands ZEC tax benefit zone. *SETT has put up €20 million ($23.4 million) of a total €45 million ($52.65 million), the rest coming from Mexico’s Ítaca Films and investor Omega Capital, to found Ítaca Films Madrid, an international content studio. “For Ítaca Films, SETT represents much more than financing. It’s an instrument which institutionalises the industry, strengthens producers and shows that creativity, when it counts on structure and solid bases, can grow and develop better,” says Ítaca’s Santiago García. *Focused on the creation, ownership and global distribution of kids & family IPs, Amuse Labs, a new Canary Islands animation company, has received a €6.4 million ($7.3 million) investment from SETT in return for a 48% equity position. Amuse Studios will become Amuse Labs’ second-largest shareholder. *SETT has taken a 46% equity participation for €1.1 million ($1.3 million) in Lazona Audiovisual Hub, along with Lazona (36%) and El Alamedia Estidios (13%), billed as a Madrid creation and post-production factory aiming to meet the large demand for post-production services in the Spanish capital. ‘Days of Thunder 2’: Jonathan Levine in Talks to Direct Tom Cruise in Paramount Sequel Nicole Kidman Got Warned About Marrying Tom Cruise but Fired Back: ‘I Don’t Care. title: Naomi Watts Believes Standards Have Changed for Older Women in the Industry: ‘Look at the Emmys Last Week… That’s Heartening to See’
full_text: Sep 19, 2026 2:48am PT Naomi Watts Believes Standards Have Changed for Older Women in the Industry: ‘Look at the Emmys Last Week… That’s Heartening to See’ The ‘Mulholland Drive’ star is at the San Sebastián Film Festival to screen Ben Shirinian’s ‘The Housewife,’ as well as to receive this year’s Donostia Award By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest Naomi Watts Believes Standards Have Changed for Older Women in the Industry: ‘Look at the Emmys Last Week… That’s Heartening to See’ 3 hours ago Catalonia: A Dozen Highlights at San Sebastián, From a Time-Loop Thriller to a Singular Heist Tale and a Potential Arthouse Sleeper 1 day ago Boutique Filmes Lines Up Marina Ruy Barbosa, João Guilherme, ‘Strange Way of Life’ Breakout José Condessa for ‘The Mystery of the 5 Stars’ With Vera Egito to Direct (EXCLUSIVE) 4 days ago See All Naomi Watts Courtesy of JuanKR for PC British actor Naomi Watts , at the San Sebastián Film Festival to receive this year’s prestigious Donostia Award, spoke about opportunities in the industry for women over 50. Talking a week after Sarah Paulson told Variety about the lack of film offers following her spellbinding portrait of Marcia Clark in “The People v. O.J. Simpson: American Crime Story,” Watts said, “things have changed.” Watts recalled entering the industry late “by Hollywood standards,” starring in David Lynch’s lauded “Mulholland Drive” at 31 years old. “I was told at the beginning that I better get my skates on because it all finishes at the age of 40. And here we are today. I’m in my late 50s. Look at the Emmys last week [and] the number of women in strong categories over 50. That’s heartening to see.” Popular on Variety Related Stories Oscars: Philippines Selects Rafael Manuel’s ‘Filipiñana’ for International Feature Race Oscars: Hungary Selects Ildiko Enyedi’s ‘Silent Friend’ for International Feature Race (EXCLUSIVE) Nominees over the age of 50 included Rhea Seehorn (“Pluribus”), Jean Smart (“Hacks”), and Allison Janney (“The Diplomat”). “I do think things have changed,” she added. “Women are consumers of film and TV, and their stories should be reflected. That narrative had to be shifted. And I am grateful to be a small part of that shift.” The actor is also at the Basque festival with Ben Shirinian’s feature debut “ The Housewife .” The film, the Donostia Award Screening, stars Watts, Tye Sheridan, Luke Evans, Michael Imperioli and Lena Olin. Set in 1964 and based on a true story, the film tells the tale of a young journalist who tracks down a potential Nazi officer living secretly in New York and befriends the suspect’s charming wife. Prodded about the parallels between a film about World War II and the Holocaust and the ongoing wars today, specifically the ongoing war in Palestine, Watts said: “It’s a very, very scary time what is going on in the world globally.” “We must be vigilant, we must pay attention, and not let that happen again. Hopefully this film sparks a dialogue. We don’t give answers; we hopefully send you away with questions of how did this happen and, who do you relate with in this story, and how we can avoid this happening ever again.” “We have to tell these stories; storytelling is important, particularly now,” she reiterated, noting how she vows to continue supporting minorities and representation on screen. “I’m proud to be a part of the LGBTQ community. Minorities are being attacked right now, and it’s frightful and unacceptable. My heart is with these communities, particularly my family. I’ll do whatever I can to stick up for minorities.” As for playing an immigrant in the U.S. as an immigrant to the country herself, Watts said she “moved to America with hopes and dreams,” all of which she has already “surpassed.” “Hermine, the woman I play in this story, was there post-World War II, when things were much more sunny and bright. Her story was about trying to find a new place and erase the past, which she was able to do for a period of time.” “In terms of me, I have American children, I do love America, and what’s going on today is complicated and certainly nerve-wracking, but I have faith that things will work out in time,” she added about the U.S.’s current political climate. Watts noted how the role was “very complicated,” and she had a “huge amount of fear” when taking on the adaptation of the harrowing true story. “It was like nothing I ever played before: this duality of this woman who had done horrific things, heinous crimes, and yet blending into society as a normal person – very much a good citizen, a good wife, baking cookies, showing up to church. That duality and living with that secret was interesting to me as an actor.” “I am always looking to do new things even though I might have a repetitive theme in my work – grief and identity— things that are meaningful to me,” she continued. “This character is like nothing I’ve ever played. I’m at an age now when some might joke I’m in my villain era, but this is an extreme one and not a joke. I felt compelled to play this story.” When asked about the similarities between her role in “Mulholland Drive” and “The Housewife,” especially how both characters broach these notions of duality, Watts said both roles are “deeply psychological and confronting,” but while she didn’t particularly enjoy playing Hermine, she has nothing but wonderful memories of her time on set with the late Lynch, who died early last year. “‘Mulholland Drive’ was nothing but fun,” she said. “It was coming at a time in my life when I didn’t have any breaks after years of struggle, so every day on set was just a wonder. Getting to learn how Lynch works and directs was truly wonderful. I’ll never forget those days.” The actor called working with Lynch “an incredible break.” “I had been working to get a film role for a good 10 years before that lucky break came. I was very much a journeyman actor, working wherever I could, but I had a lot of rejection. really was quite shut down, not bringing good energy into rooms I was asked to audition in. It took someone like David Lynch to see through the veneers I had created. We had a beautiful conversation, and he gave me the role of a lifetime.” “I’m forever indebted to David Lynch; he is in my heart forever,” she went on. “This is a film that has remained in people’s consciousness for decades, and I think it really launched me because every great filmmaker saw this film.” The San Sebastián Film Festival runs Sept. 18-26. title: Naomi Watts Says She’d Like To Work With Paul Thomas Anderson & Praises The Advancements Older Women Have Made In Hollywood — San Sebastián
full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Naomi Watts Says She’d Like To Work With Paul Thomas Anderson & Praises The Advancements Older Women Have Made In Hollywood — San Sebastián San Sebastián Opens With Political Declarations And Tributes To Werner Herzog & Outgoing Festival Director José Luis Rebordinos Fatih Akin On How A Period Of Professional Crisis Inspired His Paranormal Love Story ‘Ghost Song’ — San Sebastian View All September 19, 2026 2:26am Naomi Watts ANDER GILLENEA / AFP via Getty Images. “I started, by Hollywood standards, quite late,” Naomi Watts began this morning when quizzed on whether the treatment of older women in Hollywood has improved during a press conference at the San Sebastián Film Festival. The British-Aussie actor is at the Spanish festival to receive an honorary Donostia Award for career achievement. “I launched with Mulholland Drive , and I was 30 or 31,” Watts continued. “And I was told that I better get my skates on because it all finishes at the age of 40, but here we are today. I’m in my late 50s now.” Watts continued to praise the improvements in the Hollywood industry that have prolonged women’s careers. Related Stories News San Sebastián Opens With Political Declarations And Tributes To Werner Herzog & Outgoing Festival Director José Luis Rebordinos News Fatih Akin On How A Period Of Professional Crisis Inspired His Paranormal Love Story 'Ghost Song' -- San Sebastian “Look at the Emmys just last week, there were a number of women in strong categories over 50, so that’s heartening to see,” she said. “I do think things have changed. Women are consumers of film and TV. Their stories should be reflected. Everybody needs to see their story reflected in storytelling, so that narrative had to be shifted, and I’m grateful to be a small part of that shift.” Watch on Deadline Here in San Sebastian, Watts is also joined by her Housewife cast and director, Ben Shirinian. The film will screen this evening at the festival following Watts’ Donostia Award presentation. Set in 1964, The Housewife follows Hermine (Watts) and her hardworking husband Russel (Luke Evans), who enjoy a seemingly normal life in New York City — until the fateful day Hermine meets The New York Times journalist Joseph Lelyveld (Tye Sheridan). Following a tip from a Holocaust survivor, Joseph is investigating the possibility that Russel might be a Nazi in hiding. As his inquiry deepens — and his exchanges with Hermine become increasingly intimate — Joseph discovers a series of revelations far stranger and more complicated than he could have imagined. Watts described the role as a challenging “mind twister.” “The storyline was compelling. It is based on true events, and so it really drew me in,” she said. Elsewhere during the press conference, Watts was asked whether she had any professional goals or directors that she’d still like to work with. She responded: “Paul Thomas Anderson is someone I’ve wanted to work with for a long time.” Anderson debuts his next feature, a concert filmed at Carnegie Hall with Geese frontman Cameron Winter, next month at the New York Film Festival. A24 will release that film in cinemas. title: Writer-Star Berto Romero, Director Javier Ruiz Caldera Unpack San Sebastian Buzz Title ‘5 More Minutes’: ‘Characters and Audience Should Feel Every Second’s Weight’
full_text: Sep 19, 2026 1:38am PT Writer-Star Berto Romero, Director Javier Ruiz Caldera Unpack San Sebastian Buzz Title ‘5 More Minutes’: ‘Characters and Audience Should Feel Every Second’s Weight’ By Anna Marie de la Fuente , John Hopewell (L-R) Berto Romero, Javier Cámara, '5 More Minutes' Credit: Quim Vives World-premiering in San Sebastián main competition, Javier Ruiz Caldera’s time-warping drama ‘5 More Minutes’ (‘5 Minutos Más’) suggests one way an on-the rocks relationship may come closer together again: by plunging them into the makings of a global apocalypse. Writer-star Berto Romero (“The Other Side”) and Belen Cuesta (“The Endless Trench”) play a couple who are trying to repair their frayed marriage, retreating to an idyllic vacation home in Spain’s exquisite Girona countryside. There they are handed the keys by Carlos, a property manager, played by the ever-popular Javier Cámara (“Talk to Her”) in a rare, less simpático role. Not long after he hands over the keys, time jumps back five minutes. Related Stories John Turturro Has Waited 40 Years for an Oscar Nomination. ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Makes the Case 'I Play Rocky' Premieres at TIFF: A Movie About a Best Picture Winner That's a Best Picture Contender? Actor-writer Berto Romero and Belen Cuesta in ‘5 More Minutes’ QUIM VIVES As time continues to jump back for them, again and again, they grow increasingly paranoid. Catalonia has always looked to France for inspiration. This is a film which melds the great French and Catalan tradition of questioning the civilized manners of the bourgeoisie, rcast in a thouroughly modern genre blender, part excriciating comedy, part min-bending sci-fi, and part a shockingly violent thriller, driven by the logic of nightmares. Popular on Variety A potential breakout, “5 More Minutes” is produced by Movistar Plus, El Terrat, part of The Mediapro Studio, and Ikiru Films. Filmax handles domestic distribution in Spain and internatonal sales. Ruiz Caldera and Romero both spoke to Variety in the run-up to San Sebastian’s world premiere. What was it about this project that compelled you to take it on, particularly after your previous film? Ruiz Caldera: I always want my next film to differ from the previous one and present a new challenge. Berto Romero’s script offered that, combining the genres I love most: fantasy, thriller and irresistible humor. I immediately wanted to make it. The choice of music framing the film is striking. What informed the decision to open and close with Roy Orbison’s “In Dreams,” and what did you hope that musical motif would evoke? Ruiz Caldera : Finding the right song was difficult. We wanted something hypnotic and mysterious that signaled this wasn’t simply a comedy. Then “In Dreams” clicked. Many will remember it from David Lynch’s “Blue Velvet,” and I hope that association adds an intriguing layer. The performances feel remarkably spontaneous despite the film’s highly choreographed structure. How much latitude did you allow the actors to improvise, particularly Belén Cuesta, whose role is especially dialogue-heavy? Ruiz Caldera : We rehearsed extensively and improvised during preparation, but the actual takes were highly choreographed. The film consists of five-minute takes, so everything had to be timed precisely. Making it look spontaneous was the goal, and Javier Cámara, Belén Cuesta and Berto Romero made that possible. The film navigates an unusually delicate tonal terrain between black comedy, suspense and the fantastic. How did you calibrate those elements without allowing one to undermine the others? Ruiz Caldera : Humor helps release tension before catching the audience off guard again. Given the characters’ extreme situation, black humor also feels natural—a way of protecting themselves from anxiety and fear. The setting in Girona plays a significant atmospheric role. What drew you to this particular location, and how did its familiarity and natural beauty inform the film’s darker impulses? Ruiz Caldera : It was shot in a beautiful valley in Girona, Catalonia, at a friend’s house I’ve known since childhood. It’s a paradise – an ideal setting for a nightmare. The decision to construct the film around precisely five-minute takes presents a formidable formal and technical challenge. What motivated this constraint, and how did you coordinate the cinematography, production design, costume, sound, visual effects and production teams to sustain identical conditions across every sequence? Every sequence shot had to last exactly five minutes, no more or less. We wanted audiences to genuinely feel the weight of those five minutes without relying on editing. After months of testing, every sequence was filmed at exactly 6:35 p.m., with identical light. Close coordination between cinematography, art, costume, sound, visual effects and production made the technical feat possible. How has the involvement of Movistar Plus, a producer with El Terrat and Ikiru, helped to empower “5 More Minutes” in production terms. And how should it help its distribution potential in Spain? Romero: I have worked with Movistar Plus on several productions over the years and have built a strong relationship of trust with their creative and production teams. The same is true of El Terrat, with whom I have worked in film and television for more than two decades. Together with Ikiru Films, they have supported the project from the beginning and given us complete creative freedom. For distribution in Spain, having Filmax on board gives us great confidence. Their experience, knowledge of the market, and ability to connect films with audiences are a major advantage. Together with the support of Movistar Plus, El Terrat and Ikiru Films, we have a strong foundation to give ‘5 More Minutes’ visibility and reach a broad audience. “5 More Minutes” blends sci-fi, survival thriller and excruciating (in the best sense) comedy. What attracts you to genre mixes? I have always been drawn to stories that blend genres. Life itself is a good example: it can move from comedy to horror, thriller or drama in a matter of seconds. To me, that feels natural. I like to follow the story I want to tell and let the genres emerge organically. I come from stand-up comedy and television, where I have worked for 30 years, so my way of seeing the world is naturally influenced by humor. At the same time, I have always loved genre stories, especially horror, thrillers, science fiction and fantasy. I think my writing is a mix of everything I enjoy, filtered through my own view of life. With ‘5 More Minutes,’ I never set out to make a comedy. But in the end, humor, much like life in ‘Jurassic Park,’ found a way. A considerable number of top Spanish directors – Rodrigo Sorogoyen, Alberto Rodríguez – use genre. Is there something about Spain or Spanish cinema which explain this predilection in auteurs? I don’t feel qualified to speak for other writers or define a characteristic of Spanish cinema. For me, it is simply a personal preference as a storyteller. I find it fascinating to use genre conventions, subvert them and take audiences somewhere they don’t expect. I think this fascination with genre is more international than uniquely Spanish, though that may just be my own bias. In my case, it is a purely instinctive and irrational impulse when I write. title: Lego’s ‘Ninjago Legends: Duskfall’ Anime-Style Shorts Premiere in Korea Ahead of YouTube Release
full_text: Sep 19, 2026 12:01am PT Lego’s ‘Ninjago Legends: Duskfall’ Anime-Style Shorts Premiere in Korea Ahead of YouTube Release By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest Lego’s ‘Ninjago Legends: Duskfall’ Anime-Style Shorts Premiere in Korea Ahead of YouTube Release 6 hours ago King Charles Denies Bombshell Book Claim That He Said World Would ‘Forget’ Princess Diana 2 days ago Ozzy Osbourne and Black Sabbath’s Final Concert Film Sets October Release Date 3 days ago See All The LEGO Group “ Ninjago Legends: Duskfall” is premiering in Korea this weekend ahead of a worldwide release on Lego ’s YouTube channel. The anime-style shorts feature some of “Ninjago’s” most beloved characters as they encounter new challenges and new battles while bringing back some familiar voices from the original show as well as “Ninjago Dragons Rising.” The series of three interconnected shorts, each three-minutes long, premiered Friday at a “Ninjago Legends” Duskfall” fan event at the Park Mall Yongsan in Seoul. The shorts will be released on the Lego Group’s YouTube channel on Saturday, Sept. 19. Related Stories Oscars: Israel Selects HIV Drama ‘Tell Me Everything’ for International Feature Race TIFF Opens With Siân Heder’s Crowd-Pleasing ‘Being Heumann’ — and Apple Has Its Next Oscar Contender The three shorts are titled “The End Begins,” directed by David Cazeaux and Charles Lefebvre, “Terminus,” directed again by Cazeaux and Lefebvre, and “Epilogue,” directed by Cazeaux, Lefebvre and Hugo Cierzniak. Popular on Variety Andrew Francis reprises his role as Cole alongside Kelly Metzger as Nya and Vincent Tong as Kai. Also returning to the franchise are Brian Drummond as Diviner and Runt, Adrian Petriw as Scott and Sabrina Pitre (the voice of Sora in “Dragons Rising”) as a reporter. In a trailer for the shorts series, it opens with a female voice saying “Kai, if you make it out of this, promise me you’ll walk away.” It then cuts to plenty of action before Kai, in his red ninja outfit, says: “Save the Elementals, I’m coming.” The female voice then says: “We’re not fighting demons or monsters anymore, they call us warriors. Protectors. Ninja.” Created to mark the fifteenth anniversary of the “Ninjago” franchise, the shorts offer fans who’ve grown up the show an opportunity to watch the characters in a new way, with many hoping the anime-style shorts will be expanded into a full series. title: Portugal’s Queer Lisboa Celebrates 30th Anniversary With Vast Showcase of Latest LGBTQ Titles, Dose of Radical 1970s Counterculture and Family Fare
full_text: Sep 18, 2026 11:44pm PT Portugal’s Queer Lisboa Celebrates 30th Anniversary With Vast Showcase of Latest LGBTQ Titles, Dose of Radical 1970s Counterculture and Family Fare Unspooling are films by Ira Sachs, Leah Nelson, Pedro Almodóvar, Jane Schoenbrun, Sally Potter, the Wachowskis and João Paulo Ferreira By Ed Meza Plus Icon Ed Meza @edmezavar Latest Portugal’s Queer Lisboa Celebrates 30th Anniversary With Vast Showcase of Latest LGBTQ Titles, Dose of Radical 1970s Counterculture and Family Fare 6 hours ago Don Palathara’s Indian Drama ‘Monkey Play’ Selected for Vancouver’s Inaugural Works-in-Progress Lab (EXCLUSIVE) 18 hours ago Canada’s BetterHalf Films Joins Indonesia’s Studio Amarana on Animated Film ‘Galeo of the Seawalkers’ (EXCLUSIVE) 18 hours ago See All André Godinho's 'Nothing Left' world premieres at Queer Lisboa. Courtesy of Terratreme Celebrating its 30th anniversary this year, Portugal’s preeminent Queer Lisboa – International Queer Film Festival kicked off Friday with a vast program showcasing the latest in LGBTQ cinema, from established filmmakers to new voices, and a look back at the underground counterculture and revolutionary works of activist filmmakers on both sides of the Atlantic. Lisbon’s oldest film festival, Queer Lisboa launched in 1997 at the Cinemateca Portuguesa as the Lisbon Gay and Lesbian Film Festival, opening with the 1950 short film “Un chant d’amour,” the only film ever directed by French novelist and playwright Jean Genet, whose works included “Querelle de Brest,” famously adapted by Rainer Werner Fassbinder. Related Stories Inde Navarrette Sets Best Actress Oscar Campaign for ‘Obsession’ as Focus Features Mounts Full Awards Push (EXCLUSIVE) Telluride Toasts Andrew Haigh as 'A Long Winter' Hands Fred Hechinger and Caitríona Balfe Awards-Worthy Roles Ana David and João Ferreira Credit: Joana Linda/Nuno Ferreira Santos The festival’s origins at the Portuguese Cinematheque is one of the factors that has distinguished it from other queer festivals across Europe, Queer Lisboa artistic director João Ferreira tells Variety . Popular on Variety “From the very beginning, I would say that the festival was not envisioned as a kind of niche or festival only for the LGBTQ community because of the institutional support that it already had from day one. So I think it’s a very particular case for a queer festival in Europe. It was certainly not the case with some festivals that started more or less at the same time, like Madrid or Paris. “The audience was from the very beginning, a very broad audience and an audience interested in film, a cinephile audience,” Ferreira adds. “But of course, also because in the first three years it was organized by the Portuguese chapter of ILGA [the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association], it also had this very important community aspect to it.” The Man I Love Courtesy of Cannes Film Festival The festival’s perception of queer cinema has never been based merely on narrative, Ferreira notes. “It was much broader than that. We were interested in a queer gaze at the world. We were interested in a camp aesthetic. So we were looking for very different kinds of films that could fit in this idea.” It was a view that shaped what the festival ultimately became, he adds. “Then the festival was called the Gay and Lesbian Film Festival, but the idea was already queer at the time, the way we looked at film.” With a total of 94 feature, documentary and short films, the 30th edition of Queer Lisboa takes place at its regular venues, the Cinemateca Portuguesa and Cinema São Jorge, running Sept. 18-26. Boasting a strong lineup that includes some of the year’s top LGBTQ titles, the festival opens with the Portuguese premiere of Rami Malek -starrer “ The Man I Love ” from Ira Sachs, whose previous films, “Passages” and “Peter Hujar’s Day,” likewise screened in Lisbon. Leah Nelson’s acclaimed animated drama “ Tangles ” closes the event. Papaya ‘Papaya’ was among the first films to receive Screen Brasil distribution support. Credit: Priscilla Kellen With nearly a dozen sections, including five competition categories and six non-competitive sidebars, the festival offers a broad showcase. New this year is Queer Family, dedicated to kids and their families, with a focus on culturally enriching independent films that explore themes of inclusion and identity. Two Brazilian features make up the program, Allan Deberton’s Berlinale award-winner “ Gugu’s World ” and Priscilla Kellen’s animated “ Papaya .” It’s been a long-standing goal to attract younger audiences, says Ana David, programmer and director at Queer Lisboa. Gugu’s World Courtesy of Jamille Queiroz The new section is aimed directly at families and the festival has already received positive feedback from interested parents. “We’ll see if it’s the kids bringing their parents, or if it’s the parents bringing their kids. It’s important for us to work with young audiences who will also become the adult audiences of the festival in the future,” David says. The new section also provides the opportunity for parents and their children to have an intergenerational experience and to even talk about things after the screening, she adds. The festival has already sold a large amount of tickets for the Queer Family screenings. “We think it’s going to work out really well,” David says. With the increasing growth and appeal of LGBTQ cinema, Queer Lisboa has sought to find a balance between popular mainstream works, new discoveries and the more radical experimental films that have long defined queer cinema. “We want this spectrum, the big films and very small films,” says Ferreira. “It’s part of our joy as programmers to discover these smaller and more independent, sometimes more DIY filmmakers and filmmaking, and we try to put all that in the program. It is challenging.” While it’s much easier now to acquire films than it was 30 years ago, it’s become more difficult to filter through the huge amount of available titles and curate the 90-plus films that the festival presents, Ferreira adds. Bound Courtesy of Queer Lisboa Offering a rare treat for its 30th anniversary is an expanded Retrospectives section with 19 titles, including such works as the Wachowskis’ 1996 debut film “ Bound ”; Sally Potter’s “ Orlando ” (1992), Lisa Cholodenko’s “ High Art ” (1998), Patrice Chéreau’s “ The Wounded Man ” (1983), Kim Longinotto and Jano Williams’ British doc “ Shinjuku Boys ” (1995) and, from West Germany, Frank Ripploh’s 1980 classic “Taxi to the Toilet” (“Taxi zum Klo”). This year’s showcase is especially interesting as Queer Lisboa is hitting 30 at the same time BFI Flare in London turns 40 and San Francisco’s Frameline turns 50, David notes. Those festivals, along with Paris’ Chéries-Chéris, “served as inspirations for the birth of Queer Lisboa.” “It speaks to the longevity of queer cinema, but also the festivals that have for a long time now been promoting and expanding on the knowledge and appreciation of queer cinema,” David notes. Orlando Courtesy of Queer Lisboa For Queer Lisboa, it was an opportunity to look back at early films that are rare exhibitions in Portugal even if they’re already considered canon films within queer cinema. “We wanted to offer some classic titles that people know and can engage with the retrospective, but then also offer something new for them to learn about and that can expand on their knowledge,” David adds. An important element of that is to present the films in restored or digitized versions. It’s the first time that “Orlando” screens at the Cinemateca Portuguesa, David points out. “And they actually have a 35mm print, so it’s amazing that we can offer an excuse for this film to be shown.” “And to take it out of the closet,” Ferreira quips. Fatucha Superstar Courtesy of Queer Lisboa Also presented will be a newly restored version of João Paulo Ferreira’s 1976 subversive queer musical comedy “Fatucha Superstar,” inspired by Andrew Lloyd Webber’s “Jesus Christ Superstar.” Made in the wake of the revolution that swept away Portugal’s authoritarian dictatorship, the film blasphemously ridicules in ultimate kitsch fashion one of the main pillars of the former regime, the apparition of Our Lady of Fátima and the Christian symbolism that surrounded it. Along with Óscar Alves, João Paulo Ferreira was part of the rebellious and independent gay filmmaking movement that produced the first queer films in post-revolution Portugal. Together they founded the film collective Cineground and screened their Super 8 films in Lisbon’s queer bars and night clubs in the 1970s. Maspalomas Maspalomas Film Factory Entertainment Among the returning talents and exciting discoveries this year are Portuguese filmmaker André Godinho and the world premiere of his debut feature “Nothing Left,” described as a Portuguese queer version of “Punishment Park”; and German artist duo Benjamin Ramírez Pérez and Stefan Ramírez Pérez with the world premiere of “Life Is About Losing Everything,” their hybrid doc on the life and work of Canadian poet Lynn Crosbie, likewise a first feature. Both films unspool in the Queer Art Competition, which showcases experimental, boundary-busting works that “explore the limits of cinematic languages, genres, and narratives.” Other highlights include Swiss-French feature “ Summer Drift ,” by Céline Carridroit and Aline Suter, and the European premiere of “Public Access,” David Shadrack Smith’s look at the people who transformed New York City TV into a groundbreaking space for self-expression during the 1970s and 80s. This year’s diverse lineup includes special screenings of Pedro Almodóvar’s “ Bitter Christmas ” and Jane Schoenbrun’s “ Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma ,” while the fest’s non-competitive Panorama sidebar presents such recent international festival hits as “ Jim Queen “; “ Maspalomas ;” “ Outerlands “; and “ Prosecution .” Strange River Courtesy of Queer Lisboa Competing in this year’s Queer Lisboa feature film competition are: “Black Burns Fast,” by Sandulela Asanda (South Africa) “ On the Road ,” by David Pablos (Mexico) “ Strange River ,” by Jaume Claret Muxart’s (Spain, Germany) “ La Gradiva ,” by Marine Atlan (France, Italy) “ Iván & Hadoum ,” by Ian de la Rosa (Spain, Germany, Belgium) “ Julian ,” by Cato Kusters (Belgium, The Netherlands) “ London ,” by Victor Di Marco and Márcio Picoli (Brazil) “Raging,” by Ryan Machado (Philippines) The entire Queer Lisboa program can be explored here . title: ‘It’s My Most Personal Film,’ Says Director Rodrigo García Saiz of His San Sebastian New Directors Title, ‘Morro’
full_text: Sep 18, 2026 11:28pm PT ‘It’s My Most Personal Film,’ Says Director Rodrigo García Saiz of His San Sebastian New Directors Title, ‘Morro’ By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest Writer-Star Berto Romero, Director Javier Ruiz Caldera Unpack San Sebastian Buzz Title ‘5 More Minutes’: ‘Characters and Audience Should Feel Every Second’s Weight’ 4 hours ago ‘It’s My Most Personal Film,’ Says Director Rodrigo García Saiz of His San Sebastian New Directors Title, ‘Morro’ 6 hours ago James Gray’s ‘Paper Tiger’ Set to Open the 50th São Paulo Film Festival 3 days ago See All 'Morro' Courtesy of Calouma Films A dog is indeed a man’s best friend. A New Directors contender at the San Sebastián Film Festival, “ Morro ” explores the unlikely bond between a man and the dog he inadvertently adopts. It is Rodrigo Garcia Saiz ’s (“Lluvia”) sophomore feature and, by his own account, his most personal film to date. The titular Morro is a dog, reflecting Garcia Saiz’s own lifelong connection with the animal. Related Stories Oscars: Ukraine Selects 'Traces,' About Women Who Survived Sexual Assault During War With Russia, for International Feature Race TIFF Opens With Siân Heder’s Crowd-Pleasing ‘Being Heumann’ — and Apple Has Its Next Oscar Contender “I’ve always had a connection with dogs and I also wanted to reflect on the violence in Mexico since I left it,” says Garcia, who now resides in Madrid. “But not so much about showing the violence itself, but about what happens to the people who stay. And how an animal that doesn’t judge, that asks for nothing but love and gives love, could help.” Popular on Variety “Morro” revolves around Mateo, a vet in rural Mexico, who lives quietly with the unresolved guilt of losing his son. In a town where violence simmers beneath the surface, his fragile routine is disrupted when he treats Morro, the injured dog of a local drug lord. Caring for the animal sparks a wordless, judgment-free bond that slowly gives Mateo a renewed sense of purpose. “So the premise is really: Who saves whom? I started researching, went into conflict zones, and discovered this story, which is loosely based on the experience of someone I met through a friend.” “At first, he was a little hesitant because he didn’t really want to tell us the whole story. But little by little, he opened up. I gradually gained his trust, and he started telling me things, and I began putting the story together with another screenwriter [Carlos Armella] and some other collaborators. It was really exciting to realize that what I had in my head actually happens in real life. So I made the story very much my own and it became a story that really came from my heart.” He’s quick to point out that his film is not about drug trafficking and violence is never explicitly shown. “The violence is more in the moral and physical context.” Finding the right dog to fit the part was a challenge as he didn’t want a trained one, but as luck would have it, he found the right dog, which bonded with his lead actor, Gustavo Sánchez Parra (“Amores Perros,” Michael Rowe’s Cannes-winning “Leap Year” ), who even took him home. “He looked a little like the dog from the story I researched. And when I saw him, I fell in love with him because he had such a beautiful expression. He could also believably be a drug dealer’s dog, but at the same time, he’s such a gentle, sweet animal.” He also chose to film in 35mm with his DP Alfonso Herrera Salcedo (“Spectre”), a bold choice. “Shooting on 35mm was also a way of going back to basics. The set became almost like a church where everyone had to be quiet. There were no cell phones because the film stock is obviously very expensive, and you can’t just improvise, especially when you’re working with an animal and such a great actor. Everyone had to be completely focused and attentive. I’m really grateful that Kodak, PhotoKem and others supported me so much, because I feel the film has a very particular spirit – and that also comes from our decision to shoot it on 35mm.” His next project is even more personal: “I’m working on a film that deals with my relationship with my father, who died on my tenth birthday.” “Morro” is produced by Calouma Films , alongside Central Films and The 42 Film. Paola Cortés (“Lluvia”) Alberto Müffelmann (“I’m No Longer Here”), Julia Cherrier (“The Intruder”) and Pablo Guerrero (“New Order”) serve as producers. The 74 th San Sebastian Film Festival runs Sept. 18-26. title: Hudson Williams Shares How “Surreal” It Was for Him and Connor Storrie to Return to ‘Heated Rivalry’ Set
full_text: Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All September 18, 2026 10:06pm Hudson Williams speaks onstage during "Making Waves With...Hudson Williams" during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Mathew Tsang/Getty Images for TIFF Logo text Hudson Williams is teasing what it’s been like on set for Heated Rivalry season two. The 26-year-old actor, speaking during a conversation at the Toronto International Film Festival , spoke about what it was like for him and co-star Connor Storrie when they went back to set on the hit queer hockey romance drama . “It was surreal to step into it,” Williams told the crowd. “We’re going to be kissing each other, brother. I’m going to be doing my fucking Russian accent to you,” he said, mimicking Storrie. Williams said it was hard for them to wrap their heads around going back and were concerned they wouldn’t be able to get right back into it. Williams pointed out that it was the first time he’d ever returned to a character on a big scale. Related Stories Movies 'The Face of Horror' Review: Kristine Froseth Sparkles, but Anna Biller's Medieval Tale Can't Stop Getting in Its Own Way Movies 'Masc' Review: A Neurodivergent Gay Man Navigates the World in a Striking and Distinctive Debut Feature Williams said much of their memory around the first season wasn’t just shooting but seeing the episodes, fans reactions and everything that’s happened in the last 10 months. But ultimately the pair decided to be “overconfident” and knew they knew their characters in and out. “We’re going to show up and it’s just going to be Ilya and Shane right back,” he said. Storrie ended up working on the first day, without Williams, and came back to tell his co-star about the experience. “He was like, ‘It was sort of weird. They were all so good that I was like, am I good? Am I in it? Am I doing the thing? Am I doing an impression of Ilya?'” Williams recalled Storrie saying. Williams told the crowd he was extremely confident that wouldn’t happen to him. “Then I showed up. I was doing the scene and there was some extras, who were clearly fans, and they’re just so perky. I was like, ‘Oh God. Oh God, am I doing a Shane impression?'” he questioned. Thankfully, Williams and Storrie were able to find their footing quickly. Williams pointed to the show’s creator Jacob Tierney continuing to the make the set feel just as small and intimate as he did when they were filming season one. It helped the the crew is still the same as the previous season. Williams also teased a bit of season two , which will mainly be based on Rachel Reid ‘s Heated Rivalry follow-up novel, The Long Game . “It’s a sad book,” he said. “If season one/book one is the yearning season, book two is external adversity and [relationship] communication problems that feel very real and human.” The actor added, “To be able to play those as Shane, [it’s] going to be frustrating and annoying to leave set [when] things are left unsaid, but hopefully it’ll make for really good TV.” THR

title: World Premiering at San Sebastián, Igor Legarreta Describes His Third Film ‘The Blind Ants’ as a Coastal Western Set in the Basque Country
full_text: Sep 18, 2026 10:00pm PT World Premiering at San Sebastián, Igor Legarreta Describes His Third Film ‘The Blind Ants’ as a Coastal Western Set in the Basque Country Based on the acclaimed eponymous novel by Ramiro Pinilla, 'The Blind Ants' is a story of survival in 1930s Biskaia By Roberto Prieto Plus Icon Roberto Prieto Latest Catalonia: A Dozen Highlights at San Sebastián, From a Time-Loop Thriller to a Singular Heist Tale and a Potential Arthouse Sleeper 1 day ago ‘Brother’s Keeper’ Director Ferit Karahan’s ‘Djinn Wedding’ Asks: ‘Can a Person Who Refuses to Acknowledge Their Own Darkness Ever Truly Change Their Fate?’ 5 days ago TIFF 2026: 20 International Titles to Track, From Feng-I Fiona Roan’s Shuhua Starrer to a Taxidermy Musical and a John Madden Parkinson’s Rom-Com 6 days ago See All 'The Blind Ants.' Photo Credit: Imanol Nabea “The Blind Ants” (“Inurri Itsuak”), the third feature by director Igor Legarreta (“All the Moons,” “When You Stop Loving Me”), had it world premiere on Sept. 18 at the 74th San Sebastián International Film Festival. Part of the Zinemira section, which is dedicated to Basque productions, the film is competing for the Irizar Award for Basque Cinema. It will be in Spanish theaters on Oct. 9, distributed by Buena Vista International Spain. Set in the Basque Country in 1930, the film tells the story of an English ship that is stranded on the shores of Biscay during a violent storm. Holding tons of valuable coal, the local people of Algorta scramble to rescue some of it in order to help them survive a harsh winter. The Jauregui family decides to risk it all and brave the unrelenting storm in order to keep some of the black gold. Their decision leads to tragic consequences that will change them forever. Related Stories Oscars: Hungary Selects Ildiko Enyedi’s ‘Silent Friend’ for International Feature Race (EXCLUSIVE) Andrew Scott Has Waited His Whole Career for a Role Like 'Elsinore.' Can Focus and the Bard Anoint Him With an Oscar? “We launched a production company in the Basque Country with a clear vision: to combine our strengths with local talent to create films that are artistically ambitious and uncompromising in their production values. We achieved this with “Inurri Itsuak”: a Basque-language film with international appeal and high production value that tells a story as deeply rooted in the local context as that of Ramiro Pinilla. Partnering with Playtime for international sales and Buena Vista for distribution in Spain will help the film reach the widest possible audience, Lazona Zinema producer Luis Ferrón told Variety . Popular on Variety ‘The Blind Ants.’ Photo Credit: Imanol Nabea “The Blind Ants” stars Urko Olazábal (Goya Award for Best Supporting Actor for “Maixabel,” nominated for Best Lead Actor for “Soy Nevenka”), Itziar Ituño (“Money Heist,” “Intimacy,” “Irati”), Josean Bengoetxea (“Balenciaga,” “Errementari,” “Loreak”), Miren Gaztañaga (“The Last Romantics,” “Ane,” “The Platform”) and Carlos Santos (“The Nuclear Bunker,” “Invisible,” “1992”). It is produced by leading Basque producer Lamia Producciones, Lamia Films, Lazona Zinema, Lazona Producciones, Buendía Estudios Bizkaia, Bruja del Norte AIE, and Sideral Cinema. It is co-produced with Caviar Antwerp. Igor Legarreta. Photo Credit: Esteban Delaiglesia Variety caught director Legarreta before the premiere. The film is based on Ramiro Pinilla’s book. Was it difficult to adapt it into a narrative film? Igor Legarreta: Adapting a novel is a double-edged sword. On the one hand, you have all the necessary materials: plot, characters, theme… But on the other hand, you have to transfer a literary universe to a very different world such as cinema. It is a long and complex process where you must try to separate yourself from the initial material, but without ever betraying it. I would like to point out that Pinilla’s novel conveys his love for both literary and cinematographic fiction, especially for the American fiction of the first half of the twentieth century. The film aims not to betray that love, and I truly believe that there are not many films with the character and visual strength of “Blind Ants.” What attracted you to the story? Legarreta: Undoubtedly, the experience that reading the novel provides. It is a literary gem that has not received the acclaim it deserves. I find many emotional connections with the story of the Jaureguis: life on the Basque coast, the small universe of the caserío [the Basque farmhouse], willpower as a weapon to continue fighting…. In the end, it is the story of a Basque family and its unwavering struggle not to lose its dignity. Did you shoot the film entirely in the Basque Country? Legarreta: Yes, the film was entirely shot in Bizkaia, in the Basque Country. We tried to preserve that coastal atmosphere. It is not for nothing that I have sometimes defined “Blind Ants” as a coastal Western. This is a big Basque period production co-produced with Belgium’s Caviar. Can you tell me about how the project came together? Legarreta: As often happens in cinema, travel companions are added little by little. The arrival of Robin (Caviar) and the subsequent incorporation of Kris and his entire team (Loom) helped us to grow the project in size and ambition. They are also part of the Jauregui family. You’ve worked with Itziar Ituño on some of your previous projects. Can you tell me about your working relationship with her? Legarreta: I’ve known Itziar since the time we were making short films at university, when she was taking her first steps as an actress and I as a director. Then, for some time, our paths separated until we met again in “All the Moons” (2021). Working with her is always a pleasure. She is a very close person, generous in her way of working, the kind of actress that is always part of the crew. Perhaps that’s why she has an enormous capacity to connect with real emotions and with real life. Tell me about the rest of the actors. Legarreta: It was a challenge to bring together a family as extensive and particular as the Jaureguis. We had to find a group of actors that could give us a real sense of family. And I think we succeeded. I had never worked with most of them, and in some way, they joined the project as we were making up that family. It has been a wonderful team that managed to take that bond beyond the filming. Any particular challenges while shooting the film? Legarreta: Half of the novel takes place during a stormy night on a cliff. When it came to filming, we decided to build a huge set to be able to shoot in the best conditions. We had to guarantee full safety in the scene, while we needed to have absolute control over all the elements. It was a real technical and creative challenge where the production design led by Mikel Serrano shines through in the film. title: Gerrit Graham Dead: ‘Star Trek’ & ‘Phantom of the Paradise’ Actor Was 76
full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn ‘VisionQuest’ Creator Terry Matalas Says No GenAI Was Used In Making Of Show: “There Hasn’t Really Been A Need” Cody Fern Recalls Filming ‘House Of Cards’ When The Kevin Spacey “Nuclear Bomb Hit” Maisie Williams Played ‘Practical Magic 2’ Character As “Sapphic Icon” Despite Sequel Omitting Book’s LGBTQ Plot View All September 18, 2026 8:28pm Gerrit Graham in 'Phantom of the Paradise' (1974) 20th Century Fox Film Corp. Gerrit Graham , the actor known for roles in Phantom of the Paradise (1974) and Star Trek , has died. He was 76. The actor died of lung disease and other health complications on Tuesday in Rhinebeck, NY, according to Variety . Born Nov. 27, 1949 in New York City, Graham trained at Columbia University, where he was head of the school’s Columbia Players theater company. He made his onscreen debut in Brian De Palma’s 1968 sophomore feature Greetings . Graham was most known for his performance as glam rocker Beef in De Palma’s 1974 rock musical horror Phantom of the Paradise . He also played separate roles in Star Trek: Deep Space Nine and Star Trek: Voyager . Related Stories Legal Deadline's L.A. Law Summit: Nina Shaw & Patricia Glaser Honored On Day Of Big Ideas, Big Insights; Watch The Video Presentations News 'Lollipop Chainsaw': Cult Japanese Video Game Getting The Live Action Feature Treatment Over the years, Graham had roles in such films as Beware! The Blob (1972), Demon Seed (1977), Used Cars (1980), National Lampoon’s Class Reunion (1982), TerrorVision (1986), Chopping Mall (1986), Police Academy 6: City Under Siege (1989), C.H.U.D. title: ‘Murderous’ Review: Neil LaBute’s New Film Is Undone by Its Overly Familiar Premise and Obvious Plot Machinations
full_text: × Skip to main content By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All September 18, 2026 7:57pm Neil LaBute's 'Murderous' Oldenburg International Film Festival Best-selling novels like Jean Hanff Korelitz’s The Plot and stage thrillers like Ira Levin’s Deathtrap , among many other works, have demonstrated that stealing another writer’s work can have fateful if not deadly consequences. Neil LaBute ( In the Company of Men , Nurse Betty ) delivers another variation on the familiar theme with his latest effort, receiving its world premiere at the Oldenburg Film Festival. Taking place in a single location and featuring but three lead performers, Murderous carries a strong whiff of such LaBute-cited influences as Joseph L. Mankiewicz’s Sleuth and Hitchcock’s Rope. Unfortunately, it doesn’t live up to those predecessors, feeling like an undernourished stage thriller whose plot machinations are far too obvious. Related Stories Movies Neil LaBute and Gia Crovatin on Making Hitchcock-Lean Indie Horror-Comedy 'Murderous' Movies Zoë Bell Is Ready for Round Two Murderous The Bottom Line Stagy and contrived. Venue : Oldenburg International Film Festival Cast : Gia Crovatin, Thomas Sadoski, Jordan Baker Director-screenwriter : Neil LaBute 1 hour 47 minutes The story, beginning with a first chapter titled “Him,” revolves around Marian (frequent LaBute collaborator Gia Crovatin), a filmmaker who made a splash with her debut effort, a femme-oriented horror film entitled “Murderous.” With her financial success signified by her gorgeously rustic home, a former mill, and the vintage red Porsche in her driveway, she’s surprised one day by the unexpected arrival of Norman ( Thomas Sadoski ), who announces that he wants to have a talk. And that he’s driven all the way from Iowa to do it. Clearly made uncomfortable by the intrusion, she eventually agrees to invite him in. It turns out that they were both students at the same time — he was a teacher’s assistant, he reminds her — and had a brief romantic relationship. He compliments her expensive new home, commenting that she seems to have no personal items or photographs. What she does have are valuable knick-knacks previously owned by such famed writers as Truman Capote and Willa Cather. Not to mention Shirley Jackson’s letter opener. It’s a wonder she doesn’t have Chekhov’s gun on display. After brief small talk in which Norman’s sorry lot in life is made clear — he has no job and no girlfriend, he admits — he finally gets to the point. “Did you think I wasn’t going to see it?” he asks about her film that won awards and put her on the map. It turns out that he had originally devised the film’s premise and the two had worked on the idea together and even collaborated on flipbooks of individual sequences, which he claims to still have “somewhere” in his possession. Needless to say, he thinks they need to come to some sort of agreement on compensation. Despite the tension, things, as they tend to do in LaBute’s works, turn sexual. When he reminds her that she cheated on him during their relationship, she takes it as a cue. “Is that what you want to make up for things? A blow job?” she asks. Norman thinks carefully for a moment before replying, “I wouldn’t hate it.” To reveal more about what happens next during the charged encounter would be too much of a spoiler. Suffice it to say that things end … abruptly. Another unexpected visitor, this time an older woman, arrives in the second chapter, “Her.” She’s Lila (Jordan Baker), who declares herself to be a big fan and simply wants some DVDs autographed, including one for her son. Again, Marian reluctantly invites the stranger in, and the two engage in a lengthy discussion about Marian’s film and the film business in general. It provides the opportunity for Marian to launch into a diatribe about the frustrations of working with clueless movie distributors and marketers, which, coming from LaBute, feels like the most personal and honest part of the film. The film drops hints about Lila’s true identity, or at least Marian’s perception of it, with the subtlety of a sledgehammer. Onstage, these plot machinations might have worked with a live audience eager to be manipulated. But they come across as forced and artificial here, and despite the best efforts of the performers Murderous feels more like an actors’ exercise than an organically plotted thriller. It never transcends its air of narrative claustrophobia and, considering its thin premise, would have benefited from a sharp cutting of its overlong 107-minute running time. Full credits Venue: Oldenburg International Film Festival Production: Hardball Entertainment, Bad Pelican, Big Time Decent Productions Cast: Gia Crovatin, Thomas Sadoski, Jordan Baker Director-screenwriter: Neil LaBute Producer: Daryl Freimark Executive producers: Gia Crovatin, Neil LaBute, Alexander Sablow Director of photography: Alexander Sablow Production designers: Rob Bissinger, Anita LaScala Editor: Bridget Durnford 1 hour 47 minutes THR
