title: The Best Films of the Fall Festivals: THR Critics’ Picks
full_text: × Skip to main content Clockwise from top left: 'Misty Green,' 'Possible Love,' 'The Debut' and 'You Can See Everything.' Courtesy of A24 (3); Courtesy of Netflix Along with Sundance in January, Berlin in February and Cannes in May, the fall festival trifecta of Venice, Telluride and Toronto almost invariably yields many of the films destined to keep percolating in the conversation from critics’ group awards in December all the way to the Oscars mid-March. This year’s crop was way lighter than usual on major contenders, but The Hollywood Reporter’ s hard-working reviews team nonetheless found plenty to love. Five of our top 13 picks are documentaries, with subjects as varied as the resistance of independent journalism in Putin’s Russia; an iconoclast of British queer cinema; a devastating new perspective on the war in Gaza; a sui generis portrait of a convicted fraud queen; and the struggles of delivery workers in New York City. On the narrative side, new vehicles for Julianne Moore, John Malkovich and Mahershala Ali gave those fine actors arguably their best roles in years, while the less widely known Rosalind Eleazar scored a star-making performance that should put her on every casting director’s radar; a giant of English realism crafted what will likely be the swan-song culmination of a glorious career; a debuting Lebanese director reinvigorated the heist genre; and a master of contemporary Korean cinema delivered a unique contemplation of the wealth and class divides. DAU (Venice) Image Credit: Phenomen Berlin At once immense and intimate, political, historical and personal, Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s loose biopic of Russian physicist Lev Lendau is the kind of shoot-for-the-moon feature that rarely happens anymore — and certainly not like this (the shoot relocated hundreds of actors and thousands of extras inside a giant simulacrum of the Soviet era, their daily interactions captured by a roving team of camera and sound technicians). Comparisons could be made to Oppenheimer or The Brutalist , but this is very much its own, highly original and cinematic labor of love, telling the tale of a brilliant man crushed by the weight of a totalitarian regime. — JORDAN MINTZER The Debut (Telluride, Toronto) Image Credit: A24 Blessed with swing-for-the-fences brio, the latest feature by Jesse Eisenberg makes for a frequently hilarious journey into the mind of an overly committed actor. Julianne Moore is a hoot as newbie thespian Mona, who starts like one of those disaffected housewives the Oscar winner has played so often in her career but turns out to be much stranger, while Paul Giamatti makes director Jerry ferocious but not monstruous. As the balance of power between them begins to shift, their scenes together are not just entertaining but thrillingly dynamic. — ANGIE HAN Furies (Venice, Toronto) Image Credit: RT Features Propelled by a raw, heart-pounding ferocity, Rami Kodeih’s Beirut-set first feature is a sharp fusion of personal desperation and political rage, as specific to Lebanon’s corruption-fueled economic crisis as it is generally, woefully recognizable. Following two sisters determined to reclaim their savings after the bank freezes their accounts, the movie infuses a time-tested genre with the offhand wiseass humor of siblings who know and love each other deeply, brought to messy, magnificent life in a pair of spectacular performances. — SHERI LINDEN Misty Green (Toronto) Image Credit: A24 Coming 12 years after Top Five , his terrific last feature as writer-director, Chris Rock delivers an enthralling character study and an insightful plunge into a milieu he knows intimately. In a star-making performance, Slow Horses ’ Rosalind Eleazar plays the title character, a Los Angeles-based actress and singer whose talent is as indisputable as her gift for self-sabotage. While attempting to restart her career, she navigates money troubles, a family crisis and an industry that rarely makes things easy. Adam Driver, Daniel Kaluuya, Anna Kendrick and Rock also star. — DAVID ROONEY My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile (Venice, Telluride) Image Credit: Venice Film Festival If part one of director Julia Loktev’s 12-hour chronicle of journalism under fire concluded with a cliffhanger, part two covers the painful aftermath of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. By that point, we’ve come to know the handful of independent reporters — most of them women accused of being “foreign agents” by Putin’s government — whom Loktev documented during the months leading up to the war, showing how they held fast to their beliefs while their homeland crumbled around them. In this second part, we watch the courageous, resourceful journos deal with forced exile, scattering across several countries and continents as the Russian state continues to pursue them for bogus offenses. It’s a gripping and essential study of persecution and resistance. — J.M. NAZA (Venice) Image Credit: Venice Film Festival It’s hard to describe all the feelings provoked by watching a film like the new documentary from No Other Land directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. Outrage, of course. Most certainly contempt, on a profound level, for the current Israeli regime and its prime minister, Bibi Netanyahu. Yet this sober and thoroughly reported bombshell of an exposé, in which two dozen IDF intelligence officers detail the systematic targeting of civilians in Gaza since October 7th — how it was carried out deliberately and with state-of-the-art precision — is above all a brave and indispensable act of bearing witness. — J.M. Possible Love (Venice, Toronto) Image Credit: Courtesy of Netflix Following the haunting 2018 masterwork that was Burning , Lee Chang-dong reaffirms his status as one of the greats of contemporary Korean — and world — cinema with this transfixing chamber drama about economic and emotional unease, throwing together two couples on opposite sides of the wealth divide. All four leads in the quiet powerhouse are superb, with especially memorable work from the wonderful Jeon Do-yeon, who won the Cannes best actress honors in 2007 for Lee’s Secret Sunshine . — D.R. Queer Edward II (Venice) Image Credit: Brenda Prince/Bishopgate Institute This wondrous documentary is comprised of footage from the set of Derek Jarman’s 1991 screen adaptation of the Christopher Marlowe play Edward II . Filled with vintage archival material that supplements the portrait of the irrepressibly charming Jarman and his talented collaborators, the film is guaranteed to induce swooning nostalgia in those who remember queer life, London and the filmmaking scene thereof in the early 1990s. But the doc also offers sadly timely history lessons about the necessity of resisting despotic, homophobic authoritarians — especially if you can do it with men dressed as nuns. — LESLIE FELPERIN Tender Loving Care (Telluride, Toronto) Image Credit: Courtesy of Joseph Lynn/Thin Man Films Ltd/Bleecker Street Revolving around a London woman ( Widow’s Bay Emmy winner Kate O’Flynn), her BFF and fellow social worker (Alice Bailey Johnson) and her aging parents (Marion Bailey and Paul Jessup), Mike Leigh’s new, and possibly last, film is warm and inviting, filled with giggles and gossip and gentle gallows humor. It’s also wrenching, with a topical urgency simmering just beneath the jovial surface: Leigh is tough-minded about what it means to look out for one another at this point in history — specifically in a country whose public services have been eroded by an ethos of self-reliance codified by Thatcher and further cemented, or perverted, by Brexit. — JON FROSCH Union Town (Venice, Toronto) Image Credit: Venice Film Festival Barbara Kopple, the documentarian laureate of the American organized labor movement, follows 1976’s Harlan County, USA and 1990’s American Dream with another complex and galvanizing film taking the temperature of the national workplace. Unsurprisingly, what Kopple witnesses in the gig economy is disheartening: a decentralized employee base at the mercy of nearly faceless ownership and mired in a struggle to get UPS, Amazon and various food delivery apps to do the right thing. It’s powerful and powerfully bleak, but Kopple always finds hope in solidarity. — DANIEL FIENBERG Wild Horse Nine (Venice, Telluride, Toronto) Image Credit: Searchlight John Malkovich does his best work in years in Martin McDonagh’s poignant, blood-dipped buddy comedy . He stars as a terminally ill CIA operative dispatched in 1973 to Santiago with the younger partner he mentored (played by a wired Sam Rockwell) to lay the groundwork for a coup to overthrow Salvador Allende’s Chilean democracy. On what seems like a whim but ends up being far more complicated, the two agents visit Easter Island, where the famous sentinel-like stone heads bear witness to violence and sorrow, summoning the CIA’s irascible head of South American operations (a plum role for Steve Buscemi). — D.R. You Can See Everything (Telluride) Image Credit: A24 In the first half of this fascinatingly intimate documentary portrait , filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim essentially embed with Elizabeth Holmes in the last weeks before her prison sentence — but it’s the second half that really kicks into gear, getting excitingly meta and almost surreal. What begins as a fascinatingly intimate peek at a deluded or disingenuous scammer reveals itself as something much more ambitious and less predictable, until we’re left to ponder what value a personal truth has at all. — A.H. Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother (Toronto) Image Credit: Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios A perfectly cast Mahershala Ali finally gets a leading role suitable for an Oscar-winning actor of his stature, playing a devout Muslim and contract killer who finds himself forced to care for his three kids after his wife dies in Bassam Tariq’s achingly human Texas-set thriller . It’s a crime story with a large, beating heart, a loving portrayal of Islam, and — rarest of all — a movie that explores the possibility of a form of masculinity that allows for the full range of human emotion. — JOURDAIN SEARLES THR

title: ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been’ Review: A Stirring Pop Doc Traces How the Great Singer of ‘He’s a Rebel’ and Other Classics Reclaimed Her Name
full_text: Sep 18, 2026 7:02pm PT ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been’ Review: A Stirring Pop Doc Traces How the Great Singer of ‘He’s a Rebel’ and Other Classics Reclaimed Her Name Phil Spector made her name...and erased it. Barry Avrich's film tells Darlene Love's extraordinary story and pays tribute to her soul-stirring talent. By Owen Gleiberman Plus Icon Owen Gleiberman Chief Film Critic @OwenGleiberman Latest ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been’ Review: A Stirring Pop Doc Traces How the Great Singer of ‘He’s a Rebel’ and Other Classics Reclaimed Her Name 11 hours ago ‘Resident Evil’ Review: Zach Cregger’s Reboot Is Funky Monster Fun, a One-Man-Against-the-Squish-Zombies Lark That Never Gets Bogged Down in Video-Game Sludge 3 days ago ‘The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd’ Review: Amanda Seyfried and Scoot McNairy Are Powerful in Tim Blake Nelson’s Twisty Dark-Side Prison Saga 4 days ago See All Courtesy of TIFF “Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been” is a documentary about one of the greatest singers in the history of pop music, but it’s also a stunning meditation on the issue of identity in pop. Darlene Love recorded her most defining songs in the early ’60s, when she was part of the Phil Spector hit factory. She led a group called the Blossoms, who Spector recruited, in 1962, to sing “He’s a Rebel,” the track that became the prototype for the Wall of Sound. The song was supposed to have been sung by the Crystals, but they were 3,000 miles away in New York, and Spector, eager to rush the song into production, figured it didn’t matter — he could just credit the Crystals (which he did), and no one would know. Related Stories Oscars: Ukraine Selects 'Traces,' About Women Who Survived Sexual Assault During War With Russia, for International Feature Race Oscars: Israel Selects HIV Drama ‘Tell Me Everything’ for International Feature Race Darlene Love sings “He’s a Rebel” with a saucy majesty that builds in power, until it becomes almost lordly in its reverence-for-the-bad-boy. (It’s no accident that Kenneth Anger, in “Scorpio Rising,” transposed the song so that she was singing about Jesus.) Her voice is as big as the Wall of Sound she helped to create. She sang lead on another Crystals track, “He’s Sure the Boy I Love,” did the background vocals on many other Spector songs — and, in 1963, sang “Christmas (Baby Please Come Home),” the greatest pop-music Christmas song ever recorded. She was credited on that one, but “The Phil Spector Christmas Album” had the misfortune to be released on Nov. 22, 1963, the day JFK was shot. The record fizzled; after a few weeks, Spector suppressed any further distribution of it. The album was essentially lost (until it was reissued by Apple Records in 1972). So even though Darlene Love had been billed on the album’s greatest track, her name remained lost as well. Popular on Variety Thirteen years ago, Morgan Neville’s documentary “20 Feet from Stardom” paid tribute to rock ‘n’ roll’s most fabled back-up singers (the majority of whom were Black), and to how they spent their careers standing in the shadows. Darlene Love was one of those singers, and she featured prominently in the film; when it won the Oscar for best documentary, it was Love who stood up at the Academy Awards and gave an indelible speech. “20 Feet from Stardom” captured a very particular situation: The artists it was about didn’t get to be stars, but the movie suggested that in an alternate universe they might have been. Darlene Love, however, has lived a special, heightened version of that conundrum. She hovered in the background, not getting the recognition she deserved. At the same time, she was a star. Not a maximal one, but if being a true pop singer means singing lead on some of the most magical recordings of the 20th century, Love did that. She was out there in front, spearheading the sound. It was her name that was erased, so in a strange way her identity got erased too. You knew that voice in your sonic bones, but it was in front of you and invisible at the same time. Darlene Love didn’t need an alternate universe (she lived in both universes), and “Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been” tracks the unique fusion of glory, injustice, fleeting opportunity, dashed dreams, resilience, and latter-day recognition that defines her story. The movie, like Love’s life and career, is a one-of-a-kind ride, and by the end you don’t just feel like you know and understand this remarkable artist. You feel closer to the center of the mysteries of pop. Love is 85 now, but in the documentary, which is built around a present-day interview with her (though there’s also a ton of great archival footage), she’s ageless. Under a wig of orange-blonde curls, her face beams, her smile dances, her laugh rings out, her personality is funky and vivid, and she simply doesn’t seem old . Love got to know Paul Shaffer when David Letterman fell in love with “Christmas (Baby Please Don’t Come)” and decided, in 1986, to feature Love singing it on his late-night show (a performance that became an annual ritual). The documentary presents Love along with Shaffer and his band in a studio of the Power Station, where she performs updated renditions of several of her key songs. Her voice is extraordinary, the force and quality of it undimmed. And Love proves a great narrator of her own legend. She knows what she was robbed of (not just credit but the life she could have had), yet she has transcended bitterness. The film’s director, Barry Avrich, takes us back to the age of radio (he pays nifty homage to it in the opening credits), when you would hear a voice coming out of that box, and the voice took hold of you. Love, born Darlene Wright in 1941, shuttled between Los Angeles and Texas and spent her first 15 years in church, dunked in gospel as much as Aretha or Ray Charles were. She joined the Blossoms in the late ’50s, and they sang backup on a host of classics, starting with Sam Cooke’s “Everybody Likes to Cha Cha Cha” and then on “Chain Gang” and “Rockin’ Robin,” “Monster Mash” and “Johnny Angel.” From there, they moved on to Phil Spector. They worked for him as back-up singers, in addition to being swapped in for the Crystals and Bob B. Soxx and the Blue Jeans, for whom Love sang lead on the sublimely lilting “Why Do Lovers Break Each Other’s Hearts.” Spector was a holy terror even then (though he was also a genius), and the name game he played with his female soul singers, moving them around as if they were interchangeable game-board pieces, was designed to do several things at once. It made Spector himself the star. (He was the first producer to do that.) It enabled him to withhold royalties. And in the largest sense, it was his (racist) way of treating all his talent like indentured servants. Love became a magnetic presence on “Shindig!,” the great rock ‘n’ roll TV show that allowed its performers to be wild and woolly (Shaffer offers a great reminiscence of it). She led the Blossoms in back-up vocals on pop songs from “Monday, Monday” to the Beach Boys’ “In My Room,” and she went on tour with the other Spector singers, falling into a serious relationship with Bill Medley of the Righteous Brothers. Onstage, she had a toothy insolence. Her career was a string of missed opportunities, including one that sounds like a conspiracy theory, though as presented in “I Know Where I’ve Been” it’s a fascinating one. Love was originally set to record “River Deep, Mountain High” for Phil Spector. At the last minute, he changed the singer to Tina Turner — and the song was, of course, a legendary commercial flop, the one that effectively ended Spector’s reign. The theory presented is that Turner’s rendition of it had too much R&B grit to succeed on the pop charts of 1966. Whereas Love, who had a much smoother pop-soul croon, would have made it a hit. Ah, the seduction of alternate-universe thinking! The documentary reveals how Spector became a creepier presence with the years and continued to shadow her, at one point buying out a contract she had with someone else. There’s no doubt that Spector’s great songs made her career, but the way he designed it they also nipped it in the bud. Love was still singing in the early ’70s (we hear her do a spellbinding rendition of “I’ll Be There”), but as the age of peak R&B wound down, so did her opportunities. She was married several times and had four children, two of whom got involved in the L.A. gang-banger scene and wound up in prison. (They have since emerged and triumphed.) Love wound up cleaning houses. Yet she was not forgotten. Bruce Springsteen and Steven Van Zandt, both fans from way back, took an interest in her (they are interviewed extensively). She wound up reviving her career by doing nostalgia-act performances on cruise ships. This ultimately led to the 1984 jukebox musical revue “Leader of the Pack,” which she was featured in as it began performances in the Greenwich Village club the Bottom Line; it became a sensation. The documentary hints that it was also successful when it moved to Broadway (which isn’t the case; it flamed out there), but Darlene Love was relaunched. And as much as that, she was recognized . The exultant Letterman performances of “Christmas (Baby Please Come Home),” featuring bigger choirs each year, helped a great deal, and so did her 2011 induction into the Rock ‘n’ Roll Hall of Fame. Suddenly, everyone knew who Darlene Love was. “I Know Where I’ve Been” completes the journey. It’s a film that leaves you staggered — at the soul-stirring splendor of her voice, at the forces of the time, both big and small, that marginalized her, and at our awareness of what might have been, which should never stand in the way of our awe at what was. ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been’ Review: A Stirring Pop Doc Traces How the Great Singer of ‘He’s a Rebel’ and Other Classics Reclaimed Her Name Reviewed at Toronto Film Festival (TIFF DOcs), Sept. 14, 2026. Executive producers: Jamila Jordan-Theus, Len Evans, Tim Drake, Randy Lennox, Jeffrey Latimer. Crew: Director, screenplay: Barry Avrich. Camera: Ken Ng. Editor: Dave Kennedy. title: Chris Brown Turns on Texas Rep. as Congressional Honor Causes Controversy
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kevin Dolak Plus Icon Kevin Dolak View All September 18, 2026 6:46pm Chris Brown arrives at London court on July 24, 2026. Courtesy of Getty Chris Brown delivered divergent statements to Texas state Rep. Venton Jones and U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett , the two Texas Democrats who honored him and Usher at the Arlington stop on their co-headlining tour, as controversy swirls around the polarizing pop star’s official recognition by the two lawmakers. On Sept. 12, Crockett took to the stage during Brown and Usher’s stop on The R&B Tour at AT&T Stadium and announced that, for the multi-platinum singer’s separate contributions to music, both artists were being recognized in the Congressional Record. State Rep. Jones was also on stage at the concert to join Crockett in the presentation and presented Brown a separate legislative recognition. The decision lit up a major controversy online, with liberal Texas Democrats’ reaction to Crockett ranging from deeply confused as to why she honored a well-known domestic abuser to red-hot rage at a decision many found to be an embarrassment. Related Stories Music Chris Brown Pleads Guilty After London Nightclub Attack Music Usher Says Diddy Has Been "Misrepresented": "I Don't Have Anything Negative to Say About Sean Combs" “We are experiencing Black joy to the highest level,” Crockett said at the concert. “And I wanted to make sure we document that at the congressional level. So let’s give it up again for Chris Brown.” Crockett has not made a public statement this week regarding the event at AT&T Stadium. But speculation has run wild as to why a lawmaker known for taking President Trump to task and equating him to an abusive partner while advocating for abortion access and diversity, equity and inclusion would go out of her way to sing the praises of someone so associated with violence against women. A New York magazine article on Friday floated several potential explanations for her reasoning, from drumming up voter support before the midterms to her eye for a post-politics career as a celebrity. Brown opted to stir the pot of controversy on social media as the growing backlash against the two lawmakers brought his name into headlines this week — inevitably dredging up his dark history of domestic abuse and legal issues that still plague the hitmaker. On his Instagram page , Brown thanked Crockett but laid into Jones after Jones, in an appearance on Don Lemon’s show, apologized to domestic violence survivors and reframed the concert appearance as having been about voter mobilization ahead of the midterms — a framing Brown suggested contradicted what happened onstage, where the midterms went unmentioned. “Thank you so much,” Brown wrote to Crockett. “I apologize for any backlash you have to deal with for awarding me. I’m not political but I move off of frequency and energy and I’m so grateful. ONCE AGAIN, THANK YOU.” “I don’t want the award anymore my brother,” he wrote to Jones. “You went on with Don Lemon and started tap dancing for them folk. Y’all keep that st. “ On a now-deleted Instagram Story, he continued, writing, “Funny thing is… Y’ALL CAME TO ME WITH THIS! NOT THE OTHER WAY AROUND. I was minding my damn business. My shows in Dallas were already sold out. I ain’t [want] to be honored because I knew some st like this would happen…” Brown was probably correct to predict the political blowback. His track record of legal trouble has dotted his entire adult life. His first foray into the court system and the court of public opinion came in 2009, when he pleaded guilty to the felony assault of his then-girlfriend Rihanna, an incident that occurred when he was still a teenager. His string of legal woes has not definitively concluded since then; a case stemming from a 2023 incident at a London nightclub saw the singer take a plea in late July so prosecutors would drop charges of assault, attempted grievous bodily harm, and a weapons charge. Brown is currently awaiting sentencing in the case. THR

title: ‘Lollipop Chainsaw’: Cult Japanese Video Game Getting The Live Action Feature Treatment

title: ‘American Horror Story’ Season 13: Everything We Know
full_text: Skip to main content From left: Emma Roberts, Frances Conroy, Gabourey Sidibe, Sarah Paulson, Leslie Grossman, Aventika and Alex Consani. Eric Liebowitz/FX Logo text Get ready horror fans, because a new season of American Horror Story is approaching, and it brings back some of the series’ most beloved characters — and the actors who play them. Created by Ryan Murphy and Brad Falchuk, AHS first debuted in 2011 with Murder House and has since taken viewers through season two’s Asylum, season three’s Coven, season four’s Freak Show, season five’s Hotel, season six’s Roanoke, season seven’s Cult, season eight’s Apocalypse, season nine’s 1984, season 10’s Double Feature, season 11’s NYC and season 12’s Delicate . Now, the anthology series is nearly back for season 13, with franchise favorites including Jessica Lange, Evan Peters, Sarah Paulson, Emma Roberts and more stepping back into the Emmy-winning series, which has become a staple of the Murphy-verse. The season is executive produced by Murphy, Falchuk, Ned Martel, Charlie Carver, Eric Kovtun, Nissa Diederich, Scott Robertson, Tanase Popa, Crystle Roberson Dorsey, Jennifer Salt and Tim Minear. It’s produced by 20th Television. Below, The Hollywood Reporter breaks down everything there is to know about AHS: 13 — from its new and returning castmembers to what Murphy has teased about the franchise’s future and the first official footage. This story originally posted Aug. 13 and will be updated through the season premiere. When Will Season 13 Be Released? Logo text After AHS: 13 was originally indicated to premiere around Halloween 2026, FX set its official release date for Sept. 24 at 9 p.m. ET / 6 p.m. PT on FX and Hulu. The season will include 13 half-hour episodes, with premiere week and week two each featuring three episodes. Following that, two episodes will be released each Thursday leading up to the 13th and final episode on Oct. 29. What Is Season 13 About? Logo text According to FX, here is the official logline: “An unrivaled 13th installment that will do justice to everyone’s most feared number. Bringing together an all-star cast, many of whom are reprising fan favorite roles, American Horror Story: 13 continues to build on the anthology’s decades-long legacy that has been streamed more than 700 million hours across the globe and spawned a legion of dedicated fans. American Horror Story has redefined the genre with various installments featuring a creepy murder house, a coven of witches, a traveling freak show, a haunted hotel and the apocalypse itself. Which iconic horrors will return to haunt the hallowed halls of 13 and what new terrors await? Light your candles, draw your pentagrams and prepare for a supreme surprise.” Murphy recently told THR , “This season is a thank you to the fans for continuing to watch.” He also teased to be on the lookout for certain nods to past seasons. “We also had a lot of the original costumes still in storage that we got to use,” Murphy said. “So there are little Easter eggs threaded around in the set decoration where fans can be like, ‘Wait, wasn’t that in season two?’ It was.” Who Is Returning for Season 13? Image Credit: Getty Images (4) Logo text A plethora of franchise veterans are returning for AHS: 13. Find out who and which seasons they’ve previously been in below. Sarah Paulson : Murder House, Asylum, Coven, Freak Show, Hotel, Roanoke, Cult, Apocalypse and Double Feature Jessica Lange: Murder House, Asylum, Coven, Freak Show and Apocalypse Evan Peters: Murder House, Asylum, Coven, Freak Show, Hotel, Roanoke, Cult, Apocalypse and Double Feature Angela Bassett: Coven, Freak Show, Hotel, Roanoke and Apocalypse Kathy Bates: Coven, Freak Show, Hotel, Roanoke, Apocalypse and Double Feature Emma Roberts: Coven, Freak Show, Cult, Apocalypse, 1984 and Delicate Billie Lourd: Cult, Apocalypse, 1984 and Double Feature Gabourey Sidibe: Coven, Freak Show, Hotel and Apocalypse Leslie Grossman: Cult, Apocalypse, 1984 and Double Feature John Carroll Lynch: Freak Show, Hotel, Cult, Apocalypse and 1984 Mat Fraser: Freak Show Mena Suvari: Murder House , Apocalypse Zach Villa: 1984 Seth Gabel: Hotel And Who Are They Playing? Image Credit: Prashant Gupta/FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection; Ray Mickshaw/FX/Courtesy Everett Collection; Michele K. Short/FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection (2) Logo text Over the past few months, Murphy has posted first looks of actors returning in character on his Instagram. This has included Jessica Lange as Constance Langdon ( Murder House ), Sarah Paulson as Cordelia Goode, aka The Supreme, ( Coven ) and Emma Roberts as Madison Montgomery ( Coven ). Speaking with Entertainment Tonight at The Shards premiere in July, Murphy further revealed more details on the seasons’ characters brings together elements from previous seasons. “Everybody thinks it’s a Coven season and it’s not. It’s all the seasons,” he said. “Sarah Paulson is playing six or seven roles. Jessica Lange is playing all four of her iconic characters. Evan Peters is playing five characters… It is like the Avengers. They all come together to defeat the ultimate evil.” Perhaps the biggest surprise for fans was Lange’s return. The actress has repeatedly said to press over the years that she would not return to the show after leaving in 2015. However, Murphy was able to convince her. He recently told THR , “It all started with Jessica [Lange] because Jessica, after we did the first four seasons, wanted to go off and do different things, which I understood completely. But I reached out to her thinking she would say no, and if she had said no, I probably wouldn’t have done it. She told me a story about how she was doing Broadway last season and she would go out after the show, and there were all of these young people who were there because they all watched her work on American Horror Story . And she was very moved by that. I said, ‘Well, that’s funny, because my idea is for you to do all four of your favorite characters.’ And she said, ‘Sign me up. I’d love to do it.’ I was so grateful.” “Before I started writing it, I had all of them — Emma [Roberts] and Evan [Peters] and Kathy Bates; Angela Bassett and Gabourey Sidibe and Leslie Grossman,” he said, in addition to Paulson. While promoting Murphy’s other series, The Beauty in January, Peters told THR that he was “shocked” Lange agreed to return: “Ryan knows how to have those dinners. He will get you in a second. I was definitely shocked, but thrilled, honestly.” ( See more details on character’s in the trailer section. ) Who Are the New Cast Members in AHS:13 ? Image Credit: Getty Images (4) Logo text First-time AHS actors include Paul Anthony Kelly, Alex Consani, Avantika, Madelaine Petsch, John Waters and Joey Pollari. Kelly most recently worked with Murphy on Love Story: John F. Kennedy Jr. & Carolyn Bessette , where he played JFK Jr. The 37-year-old actor appears with blonde hair in AHS: 13 , as far as his character, Vogue reported that he is “the linchpin of the season.” What Happened to Ariana Grande’s Role? Image Credit: Monica Schipper/Getty Images Logo text On Halloween 2025, Murphy announced on this Instagram that Ariana Grande was set to join a slew of American Horror Story veterans for season 13. However, in July, THR confirmed that the Grammy winner had dropped out of AHS: 13 due to a scheduling conflict with her Eternal Sunshine tour. Murphy recently spoke with THR about Grande’s exit, saying, “I love Ariana Grande. We’re great friends. I had an idea and I came to her and she, very immediately, said, ‘I’m not sure because I think I’m going on tour.’ I don’t think the tour had been announced, and she had obviously just finished the Wicked movie. So when it came time to do that episode, I called her up and she was like, ‘I don’t know how I’m going to juggle the tour with this.’ And I said, ‘OK, if you can’t, we can push to another season.’ She said, ‘Great.'” “You have to be respectful,” he continued. “Who is busier than Ariana Grande? No one. She had told me at the time, ‘I have this album that’s dropping.’ It was really, truly a scheduling conflict. … Ariana is a big fan of horror. She’s obviously done homages of that in her work; she did Scream Queens for me and loved the experience, and people love her in that show. So I will always work with her. I love her, and I support her. It was a very big swing, but I might bring that back for another season, per Ariana’s availability.” Has There Been a Trailer? Image Credit: FX Logo text A teaser trailer released Aug. 13 showed the franchise’s most beloved stars and characters back on screen — in addition to some of its most infamous villains. Twisty the Clown (John Carroll Lynch) from Freak Show opens the teaser, which then pans inside what appears to be a hotel, seemingly nodding to Hotel. Peters appears as Kai Anderson ( Cult ), Lange as Constance Langdon ( Murder House ), Angela Bassett as Marie Laveau and Emma Roberts as Madison Montgomery — both from Coven. Kelly is seen in a bathtub with a snake, hinting that he could be a villain, while the trailer ends with Paulson as Cordelia Goode ( Coven ) looking at herself in the mirror — which then breaks. The official trailer released Sept. 10 offered a closer look at the characters the returning stars are reprising. “Get in. It’s witch-hunting season,” Peters‘ James Patrick March from season five’s Hotel says. The trailer also confirms that Peters is reprising his first AHS character, Tate Langdon, from Murder House, as well as the Rubber Man, the sinister figure known for wearing a skintight black latex suit. Elsewhere, Lange is seen as Fiona Goode, while Sidibe appears as Queenie ( Coven ). Lourd plays Winter Anderson ( Cult ), Grossman plays Coco St. Pierre Vanderbilt ( Apocalypse ) and Lange plays Elsa Mars ( Freak Show ) as well as Sister Jude Martin ( Asylum ). What’s the Future of the Franchise? Logo text With season 13 of AHS on the horizon, Ryan Murphy has no plans to slow down. Speaking with THR earlier this month for his latest show, The Shards, Murphy made clear, “Season 13 is not the end.” “I’m working on season 14 as we speak in terms of, ‘What’s the idea?’ and ‘Who wants to be in it?'” he said. Murphy added, “I loved doing this season because I had not directed an American Horror Story since Freak Show , I think. Not since season four. And I directed the pilot this year and I just love the process of going to all the castmembers, all of whom are very busy, and saying, ‘Hey, can we get the band back together?'” Since starting the series in 2011, Murphy has emphasized his passion for AHS, as has FX boss John Landgraf. “It’s a very important show in my career,” he said. “It’s something that John said, ‘As long as you want to keep making them, I’ll keep airing them.’ That’s always been the idea behind it, which is very empowering.” Will There Be a Podcast? Image Credit: Courtesy of FX Logo text Like Murphy’s The Beauty and The Shards on FX, AHS: 13 will also have an official video podcast, AHS: 13 Official Podcast, on Hulu to accompany the season. The four-episode podcast will feature castmembers and creatives interviewing each other, with new episodes beginning with the release of the season premiere. AHS: 13 Official Podcast will be available on Hulu, Hulu on Disney+ for bundle subscribers in the U.S., Disney+ internationally, YouTube, with the audio-only version available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify or wherever you listen to podcasts. The series will be produced by FX in partnership with AT WILL MEDIA. See the release schedule, below. Episode 1 (Sept. 24): Sarah Paulson and Paul Anthony Kelly Episode 2 (Oct. 1): Emma Roberts and Joey Pollari Episode 3 (Oct. 8): Emma Roberts and Costume Designers Lou Eyrich and Catherine Crabtree Episode 4 (Oct. 15): Paul Anthony Kelly and Production Designer Anu Schwartz THR

title: Kohner Agency Lays Off Its Talent Agents Due To “Profound & Unprecedented Economic Pressures”
full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Netflix Cancels ‘Sweet Magnolias’ After 5 Seasons, Orders New Sheryl J. Anderson & JoAnna Garcia Swisher Series ‘Ladies Of The House’ HBO Lands ‘The Spread’ Starring Javier Bardem With Series Order After Big Bidding War; Miami Drama Comes From Bill Dubuque & Fifth Season Hulu Orders ‘Heatwave’ Ibiza-Set Limited Series From ‘Joan’ Creator Anna Symon View All September 18, 2026 6:13pm EXCLUSIVE : The Kohner Agency is downsizing. Its three talent agents have been laid off. The talent department will stay open to service existing contracts and collect commission only. Owner and President Pearl Wexler stresses that the agency, which has been in business for almost 90 years, is not closing. Its literary department is staying put, and Wexler herself will continue to represent acting and literary clients. “It is with a heavy heart that we must announce a restructuring of our talent representation team, necessitated by the profound and unprecedented economic pressures currently facing the broader entertainment industry,” The Kohner Agency said in a statement to Deadline, which you can read in full below. Related Stories News 'VisionQuest' Creator Terry Matalas Says No GenAI Was Used In Making Of Show: "There Hasn't Really Been A Need" Legal Paramount And State AGs Begin Preliminary Talks Ahead Of October Settlement Meetings The post-Covid, post-Peak TV industry consolidation has been particularly hard on smaller, boutique talent agencies, which have found it hard to survive with a marquee, signature client who commands a big, steady paycheck as a star on an established series. Agencies that shut down in the past couple of years include A3 and KMR. That has further limited opportunities for up-and-coming actors to get an agent. Watch on Deadline Founded by Paul Kohner in 1938, The Kohner Agency is the second oldest in Los Angeles behind WMA (now WME) with long traditions in talent representations. Its early clients include Marlene Dietrich, Greta Garbo, Maurice Chevalier, Billy Wilder, Henry Fonda, John Huston, Ingmar Bergman, Lana Turner and Liv Ullmann. Wexler has owned and run the agency for the past 25 years. Here is the statement: For nearly nine decades, The Kohner Agency has stood as a pillar of the entertainment community, founded in the late 1930s as one of the oldest talent agencies in Los Angeles and built on a bedrock of fierce advocacy, boutique dedication, and deep artistic stewardship. Throughout our history, we have navigated changing landscapes by staying true to our core mission: protecting and nurturing the finest talent in film, television, theater, and literature. It is with a heavy heart that we must announce a restructuring of our talent representation team, necessitated by the profound and unprecedented economic pressures currently facing the broader entertainment industry. This decision was agonizing, and we do not take lightly the impact it has on colleagues who have been valued parts of our professional family. We are incredibly grateful for their hard work, dedication, and contributions during their time with the agency, and we sincerely wish them the very best in their future endeavors. Moving forward, the Kohner Agency leadership will be overseeing the transition to ensure continuity for our clients as we steer the agency through these challenging times. ‘Resident Evil’ Leveling Up With Franchise-Record $50M-Plus U.S. Opening Trump Bans CNN, MS Now & Others From White House, Says More To Follow Company & State AGs Begin Preliminary Talks Ahead Of Settlement Meetings Brad Pitt Returning For ‘World War Z’ Sequel; Edward Berger Directs For Paramount Read More About: 1 Comments

title: Between ‘The Love Hypothesis’ and ‘Adults,’ Rachel Marsh’s Breakout Moment Is Here
full_text: × Skip to main content Marsh is set to star as Anh in 'The Love Hypothesis.' Photography by JJ Geiger, Styling by Katie Bofshever, Hair by Barb Thompson, Makeup by Hinako “I love anytime women are funny,” actress Rachel Marsh declares. Thankfully, the 34-year-old has been able to be in plenty of projects that showcase this, most recently Prime Video’s romantic comedy The Love Hypothesis . Marsh plays Anh, a graduate student and best friend to Lili Reinhart ‘s Olive in the streamer’s adaptation of the wildly popular Ali Hazelwood novel. The actress was not looking to become the quirky best friend character, a trope that director Claire Scanlon and writers Sarah Rothschild and Hazelwood were not interested in rehashing. Related Stories TV 'Adults' Defies Sophomore Slump With Ratings Growth Next Big Thing Xolo Maridueña Wasn't Planning to Be an Actor, But Has Been "Pleasantly Surprised by the Journey" “She is important in this story,” Marsh tells The Hollywood Reporter on a recent Zoom. “She also is funny.” Marsh feels like the friendship between her character and Reinhart’s Olive is the foundation for the entire story, something that’s also true in Hazelwood’s book. The two women had a wonderful time finding that on — and off — screen friendship. “Building that trust was pretty easy. Lili is so amazing. She’s so sweet,” the actress says. “She’s such a good actor and a great scene partner. It was really fun for us to get to develop their best friendship over the course of the summer in Montreal.” The upcoming romcom is not the first time you’ve seen Marsh on your screen. Her turn as Carly, the girlfriend to leading player Samir (Malik Elassal), in Adults has gone viral over the last month. It’s mostly thanks to a ridiculously catchy fake K-pop song in the series — if you haven’t heard “Hiccups (Body Go Crazy),” it’s time to look it up . “When I was reading it, I was like, ‘You guys know this is too good,'” she says of the song. It all started when Marsh got a call from series co-creator Ben Kronengold telling her that the show was thinking about making Carly a K-pop star and wondering if it’s something she’d be comfortable with. “I was just tears in my eyes, full body chills,” she says cheekily. “No one’s ever asked me this before. My dream.” Former Saturday Night Live video director Paul Briganti directed Marsh’s turn as a K-pop star on Adults , helping bring some SNL music parody vibes to the scene where she shoots a music video for the song. The director cheered her on as she made “the stupidest hand moves or facial expressions,” something she loved. “It sparked something in me, which I think every single girl has. Where I wondered, ‘What if I can sing and I just haven’t been vocally produced in the right way,'” she says. There’s an entire choreographed version of the song that didn’t make the cut. Maybe it’ll be released, she muses. But “Hiccups” fans, don’t worry. Marsh is also pleading for a version of the song to be released on streaming platforms. “I really think they should put the song on Spotify or something,” she says. “I think people yearn for things like that, to just have a moment of joy.” *** It’s a busy release couple weeks for you. How are you feeling? I feel good. It’s been really cool. We had our first fan screening the other night for The Love Hypothesis and it went really well. It’s fun, this waiting period. The first batch of people saw it, and they really like it. Are they going to get spoilers? I’m just anticipating a lot, but I think it went really well and it made me even more excited for the 23rd when it comes out. Did you know about the book at all before you signed on? I did. I had seen it because it was a big book in airports and bookstores everywhere. It was a top seller for so long, so think I just saw the cover and it was on my list of books to read. I never got to read it. I feel like it was beautiful that I was able to read it when I booked the job and didn’t really have a preconceived notion of it before that, so I could find the similarities between the book and the script. That was really fun I feel so honored to be in it. It’s so beloved by so many people. (l-r) Jeremy (Nicholas Duvernay), Ahn (Marsh) and Malcolm (Jaboukie Young-White) in ‘The Love Hypothesis.’ Philippe Bossé/Prime Video How was it shooting in Montreal? Awesome. I’d never been. I was like, “What is this magical place?” It felt like Europe and Brooklyn. Like other cities but nicer people and beautiful streets and public transportation. I could go on and on, but I loved it so much. Part of it is being an actor is so fun is if you’re lucky enough to book a job in a place that you haven’t been, it’s like they put you up, they pay for things. You get to experience the world in this privileged sense, but it’s such a dream. I really had a blast and I tried to do all the Montreal things. We all did Cirque du Soleil as a cast. There was such a fun food scene in Montreal too. I tried to try all the food, and I love Canada. What is the ideal genre for you? Do you like that you get to dabble in different things? I really do. In acting — it’s interesting because you don’t really get a lot of agency in choosing your jobs — but I feel so lucky. I’ve had a lot of these roles that are drama, and I came from comedy. I had some imposter syndrome for sure doing them, but then the more I did it, I was like, “Oh, comedy and drama are so…” They’re so closely linked. I don’t know, it feels really fun for me to get to do both. As long as it’s feeling fun. Fallout also has an element of comedy, so I think that feels very familiar. But then the cool thing about them is they shoot on film, so that’s such a challenge for me, it’s totally new. With The Morning Show , there’s so many celebrities in that show. It’s a very high pressure job, and so that’s a challenge in a different way. The acting is fun, and I’m just mostly coming in and delivering bad news to Jennifer Aniston, and so it’s like, “How do I do that in eight different ways?” Does it all come back to comedy? For me, comedy has always been what I am trying to be really great at, and I think it’s the most challenging thing to do as an actor. Even though I’ve done some dramatic stuff, I still think the comedy is the hardest, and so I will always want to be doing that and pushing myself to be better at it. What’s the ideal day off for you look like? I’m being honest, an ideal day off — this sounds so basic, this is not going to be good. I try to go to a workout class in the city. In Montreal, I tried to go to a fun Pilates class or something, and then I’ll try to find a coffee shop because I used to co-own a coffee shop. I love pulling my own espresso shots. I have a little espresso machine. I just love coffee, and I love buying an $8 little drinkie. I don’t know why. I just have to buy it, so I will go to a coffee shop just read a book or be on my phone or just hang out and people watch. That’s really what I did a lot in Montreal, or even in Toronto, when we were shooting Adults and I had the day off. I’m not used to being by myself very much, so it’s nice to be forced to. I try not to try to do extra work like writing or whatever when I’m shooting something because it feels like just the work is enough. [I love] just going in and eating. I love to eat dinner by myself too. I love going to a new restaurant and sitting at the bar and getting a glass of wine. Some places it’s way more chill, but if you do it in L.A., people are like, “Whoa, this girl is in crisis.” That’s crazy. There’s so many people here, you’d think it’d be more acceptable. No, you can’t. Even I am judgmental of girls who do that, but in any other city, anywhere else in the world, I feel like it’s totally fine. I took advantage of that, and nobody even cares or bothers you. I would bring a book or just sit there and talk to people. I like to do that a lot or just watch TV. In Canada, they have a very interesting TV choices, so I got a VPN and had to do that to watch my shows. Just a chill day by myself is really nice. Marsh as Carly in ‘Adults’ season two. FX You used to co-own a coffee shop? Oh my God, girl. Please tell me more. Well, when I got out of college… I went to business school, and I didn’t even know I wanted to be an actor. I grew up pretty religious. I don’t know if you want to put this in there, but pretty religious and really wanted to do good in the world. I guess that’s not a religious thing, but I worked at a couple nonprofits and worked for an agency that worked for nonprofits. I was really in the nonprofit space, and then I got burnt out by that, which sounds so insane. I got burnt out by the nonprofit life and thought about what I wanted to do. I was already selling my homemade almond milk to this coffee shop here in L.A. Then I just became a co-owner. We worked at the coffee shop together, and we had regular customers. I still am friends with a lot of those people. I had worked in restaurants and stuff before, but never a coffee shop, which I think is a very specific thing for L.A. culture. The service industry, in current day, is rough. I know how specific I am with my coffee or my matcha, so I understand some people, but it was rough. I really did love it. I loved having a little business. Maybe one day, I’ll own another coffee shop or a little shoppy shop, something where I could sell stuff. We’ll see. Maybe I won’t act forever, or maybe I will and it’ll be a tax write-off. THR

title: Paramount And State AGs Begin Preliminary Talks Ahead Of October Settlement Meetings
full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten , Dade Hayes September 18, 2026 4:44pm Story Arc L-R: Rob Bonta and David Ellison Getty Images They’re talking! Or are they? And what are they actually talking about? Does everyone need to chill out? Paramount and state attorneys general are talking, we are told. However, the discussions that are occurring over coming to a deal in the battle over Paramount’s $111 billion merger with Warner Bros Discovery are far from advanced. Related Stories Legal Paramount Sets California Exit Plans Over Antitrust Battle With Blue States & Stymied $111B WBD Merger News Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger Clears FCC Foreign Ownership Review In fact, sources tell us, the conversations that are occurring between David Ellison ’s team and California AG Rob Bonta ’s crew are centered on laying out the agenda for their already scheduled mid-October court ordered settlement discussions. “This is part of the process before you get the principals onboard, it’s pretty straightforward,” declares an individual with direct knowledge of the state of affairs. “The end is not nigh.” Earlier this week, a federal judge made it official and ordered Para, WBD and the AGs to appear for a two-day settlement conference October 14-15 in a San Francisco courtroom. Watch on Deadline Core to the discussions will be scenarios like Paramount potentially operating the film and TV studios of Paramount and Warner Bros. separately, at least for a period of time after the close. Bonta has said a “behavioral remedy” like the company agreeing to release at least 30 films a year, will not satisfy the plaintiffs. Along with studio consolidation, cable network concentration is a key part of the states’ complaint, with speculation centering on some way of moving some of the 50-plus cable networks out of the combined portfolio to avoid running afoul of antitrust limits. Eyebrows (and hopes) were raised late Friday about a potential resolution of Paramount’s legally waylaid WBD merger. The Wall Street Journal reported tonight that Paramount is in “advanced talks” with California’s Bonta over a settlement of the antitrust suit being brought by the Golden State AG and 11 other states. Shares in Paramount, which are down 23% in 2026 to date amid mounting uncertainty about the fate of the merger, jumped 5% in after-hours trading. WBD stock, which is also underwater for the year, rose 6% after hours. After Donald Trump’s DOJ and other major jurisdictions approved the mega-merger with no conditions, the dozen attorneys general filed a much-expected antitrust suit against Para and WBD on July 13. The case, set to go to trial on March 2, 2027, has seen an explosion of threats that Paramount would move to a red state , “blackmail” accusations by Bonta and a media war in the court of public opinion. It could also cost Ellison and his Oracle founding father Larry Ellison some sweet cash with a $7 million a day ticking fee set to WBD shareholders to start on October 1. In that context, talk of advanced talks is just another piece of that PR puzzle. “I get why some want this to look bigger than it is, there’s a lot of pressure here,” an insider notes. “This is too big, too much on the line for anyone to rush a deal,” the source added. “Hold your horses. No one wants to waste anyone’s time.” As with initial talks last month, it is mid-level staff that are in communication as the brass stay above the fray, as it is, we hear. Paramount had a blunt “no comment” on whether negotiations with the AGs were going on and what the status of them are at present. Having called out Paramount previously for alleged leaks that scuttled the last set of behind the scenes talks, Rob Bonta’s office today were 100% by the book. “Potential settlement talks are confidential,” a spokesperson for the CA AG told Deadline In the non-answer answer they added: “We cannot confirm or deny whether settlement talks are occurring or their alleged substance.” Interestingly, Bonta’s office did not complain of leaks or bad faith on the part of Paramount like they did last month when planned settlement talks were cancelled on claims the company was playing the press. While there appeared to be reason for optimism (mild as it is at this stage) there are many caveats to consider — and not just because there is a big Paramount+ streamed UFC fight out of L.A. this Yom Kippur weekend. Getty Images The latest word of discussions follows an ill-fated sequence in August. Bonta canceled negotiations hours before they were set to take place, accusing Ellison of “playing games” ahead of those meetings. “Not only did Paramount leak the alleged substance of settlement discussions, but they misrepresented these discussions, demonstrating a lack of good faith,” Bonta said at the time. Even as recently as Thursday of this week, when Bonta made an appearance at the Atlantic Festival in New York, the top cop of California said the fate of the deal “lies at the feet” of Ellison and the Paramount team. A follow up sit-down on MS Now, Democrats’ favorite cabler newser, contained much of the same even as Paramount leaks tried to up the ante on the Melrose lot packing up for Tennessee, Texas or Georgia. Sources tell us Bonta had a “conversation” with fellow ParaBros antitrust plaintiff NY AG Letitia James while out on the East Coast this week. To that, it is not clear if AG Bonta is back on the West Coast tonight. The leverage has been heavily on the side of the AGs since a string of rulings in the case by a federal judge favored the plaintiffs. Even when it came to setting a date for the antitrust trial, the judge landed on early March, which was a lot closer to the AGs’ preference of April than to Paramount’s stated desire for November. Despite momentum in the case, high-profile Democrats in California, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and L.A. Mayor Karen Bass, have publicly pressured Bonta multiple times to settle the case. The ambitious Newsom and reelection-fighting Bass fear damage to the industry, L.A. and the state if the deal remains pending for several months. At the same time, of course, a damning August report delivered to L.A. County from the region’s Department of Economic Opportunity says the $80 billion debt ladened merger will likely cause the loss of thousands of jobs , adding to the pain for a region already facing a downturn in production and other headwinds. The job loss and economic pain could be much greater if Paramount makes good on their threat to leave L.A., says a September 10 report to the County from the Economic Development Corporation. On the flip side, that same leaked EDC report, which Paramount commissioned, also told the powerful Board of Supervisors that ailing Hollywood would be boomtown if ParaBros went though with jobs and productions galore. As well, the ParaBros court calendar is looking pretty full even before those official settlement talks of next month and the spring 2027 trial. A hearing will be held next week in Oakland on Paramount’s request for a $1.88 billion bond from the plaintiffs to cover “extraordinary losses” the company anticipates due to having to pay those pricey ticking fee during litigation. title: Paramount and California AG Reportedly Closing in on a Settlement
full_text: Skip to main content By Winston Cho Plus Icon Winston Cho View All September 18, 2026 4:20pm Getty Images Logo text Paramount and a dozen states led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta are closing in on a deal to settle a lawsuit challenging the studio’s bid to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday. The two sides are in “advanced talks” to resolve the case, per the report. Under the reported deal, terms include “Paramount agreeing to operate the two companies’ movie studios separately for a period rather than immediately combining them.” In another sign that a deal is imminent, Reuters reported that an agreement could come “as soon as this weekend.” The settlement could require independent content monitoring of CNN, plus a commitment on the number of theatrical releases. Across the litigation, Bonta has maintained he’ll only accept structural remedies, which typically involve companies selling off parts of the combined business, and has previously said such an agreement to run studio operations independently cannot be the primary component of any potential deal. So far, Paramount has only offered behavioral concessions, including a pledge to release at least 30 movies with 45-day theatrical windows. A deal struck without any divestitures would be a major win for Paramount CEO David Ellison, who’s threatened to move the studio out of California if an agreement isn’t reached by the start of next month regardless of the ultimate outcome of the case. With a settlement, Paramount would be able to close the merger ahead of an Oct. 1 deadline when a $7 million-per-day so-called ticking fee will start to accrue. The discussions are “ongoing and there is no guarantee that an agreement will be reached,” the story added. “Potential settlement talks are confidential,” said a spokesperson for Bonta’s office in a statement. “We cannot confirm or deny whether settlement talks are occurring or their alleged substance.” Paramount declined to comment. Movement on deal talks has been slow, with leaks having blown up discussions in public jockeying over a settlement. Last month, Bonta canceled a meeting with Paramount scheduled for the following day, accusing the studio’s representatives of leaking and misrepresenting details of negotiations they held. A trial is scheduled to start in March, with Paramount, the states and the Writers Guild of America slated to formally sit down for two consecutive days starting Oct. 14 to explore a settlement. A key regulatory approval came on Thursday when the FCC signed off on equity investments from three prominent Middle East sovereign wealth funds that are backing Paramount’s bid. The sovereign wealth funds are collectively providing roughly $24 billion in financing to help bankroll Paramount’s bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, according to SEC filings. Their investment, along with that of others, will result in foreign investors collectively holding 49.5 percent of the combined company. THR

title: John Wilson Lays Down ‘The History of Concrete’ With ‘The Weight’, ‘Shaun The Sheep’ In Packed Indie Weekend – Specialty Preview
full_text: Skip to main content By Jill Goldsmith Jill Goldsmith Co-Business Editor More Stories By Jill AG Bonta Says Paramount’s California Exit Is David Ellison’s Choice: “It Lies At Their Feet” Steven Paul Talks U.S. Production Incentive And “Uplifts” To Sweeten Deal As Draft Legislation Takes Shape James Cameron’s Lightstorm Vision Acquires Creative-Tech Collective Outsyders View All September 18, 2026 4:15pm The Weight and A History Of Concrete and Shaun the Sheep- The Beast of Mossy Bottom Vertical/John Wilson/Ardman It’s a busy specialty weekend with fewer new studio releases. Well-reviewed Depression-era western The Weight starring Ethan Hawke and Russell Crowe in wide release joins comedic doc The History of Concrete by John Wilson in an exclusive engagement. GKids opens Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom and Johnny Knoxville stars in R-rated Tiny Fugitives . From TIFF come Angelina Jolie’s drama Without Blood and doc You Had to Be There (full title below), about how a 1972 Toronto production of the musical Godspell changed the comedy world. Related Stories News The 65 Movies That Have Made More Than $1 Billion At The Global Box Office News 48 Of The Most Anticipated Movies Of 2026 The Weight from Vertical opens in wide release on 1,504 screens. Director Padraic McKinley’s feature film debut stars Ethan Hawke and Russell Crowe. Certified Fresh at 93% on Rotten Tomatoes, it premiered at Sundance, see Deadline review . Opened the Deauville Film Festival this month, with Hawke receiving the Deauville Talent Award celebrating exceptional artists in cinema. Watch on Deadline Referenced as harkening back to classics such as William Friedkin’s Sorcerer and John Huston’s Treasure of the Sierra Madre , The Weight is set in 1933 Oregon as Samuel Murphy (Hawke) is torn from his daughter and sent to a brutal work camp. Warden Clancy (Crowe) tempts him with early release if he smuggles gold through deadly wilderness, but betrayal festers within the crew, and Murphy questions how far he’ll go to see his child again. Preview events this week included an AMC Dolby Cinema Early Access screening program at 200+ theaters and an Alamo Drafthouse simulcast screening across the chain’s markets followed by a live Q&A with Hawke, co-star Julia Jones and McKinley from the Brooklyn location. Magnolia Pictures drops Sundance-premiering The History of Concrete by the host of HBO series How To with John Wilson at the IFC Center in New York. The comedic documentary is loosely structured around and inspired by cement, the world’s most widely used building material and the bedrock of Wilson’s beloved New York City. He bounces from Rome to check out the Pantheon, built in 126 AD (the world’s largest unreinforced concrete dome), to a concrete convention in Vegas, with long digressions into Hallmark moviemaking, tattoo taxidermy and New York’s underground music scene — interspersed with musings on his career path and Zoom meetings with perplexed potential investors in the project. Wilson’s HBO series ran for three seasons from 2020-23. The History of Concrete sits at 100% RT score (off 41 reviews). Based on presales, it’s looking like the best opening for a documentary in IFC’s 21-year history, per Magnolia. The distributor went heavy on the NYC premiere Wednesday with a concrete truck wrapped in the film’s title treatment parked outside the theater, and a 125-pound poster made entirely from concrete in the lobby. Expands to 20 markets including Los Angeles next week. Greenwich Entertainment is out with You Had To Be There: How the Toronto Godspell Ignited the Comedy Revolution, Spread Love & Overalls, and Created a Community That Changed the World (In a Canadian Kind of Way ) by Nick Davis at Film Forum in NYC. Eugene Levy, Martin Short, Jayne Eastwood and others reminisce about the 1972 Toronto production of the musical Godspell , where Short, Levy, Gilda Radner, Victor Garber, Paul Shaffer and other entertainment icons got their start. Premiered at TIFF. See Deadline review. Executive produced by Judd Apatow. Adds L.A. and other markets next week. Without Blood from Brainstorm Media, directed by Angelina Jolie and starring Salma Hayek and Demián Bichir, opens on 350 screens. Jolie also produced and penned the screenplay based on the book by Italian writer Alessandro Baricco. A young woman seeks a reckoning decades after surviving the brutal murder of her family during a wartime conflict. Premiered at TIFF, see Deadline review . Moderate/wide : GKids is releasing StudioCanal and Aardman production Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom on 2,173 screens. The film is currently Certified Fresh at 98% on RT. Official synopsis: The residents of Mossy Bottom Farm are looking forward to Halloween – until the clumsy Farmer trashes the Flock’s beloved pumpkin patch. When Shaun turns mad scientist to fix the problem, things rapidly spiral out of control… With The Farmer missing and a wild beast roaming the woods of Mossingham, all the ingredients are in place for a monstrously fun family adventure. Indie distributor Inaugural Entertainment opens the raunchy R-rated comedy Tiny Fugitives , starring Johnny Knoxville, in about 300 theaters. Co-written and directed by Michael Lewen, it follows a reckless, fiercely determined group of 12-year-olds who hatch a chaotic plot to escape reality and spend the rest of their lives at sleepaway camp. Standing between them and permanent freedom is Bob (Knoxville), the camp’s deranged, relentless, 50-year-old lifer counselor. With Aaron Harris (Matlock) , Isa Bernal Steiner, Jai Soundar, Alyssa Gervasi, with Blake Anderson (Workaholics) and Jay Baruchel (How to Train Your Dragon) . Sundance-premiering The Musical by Giselle Bonilla, written by Alexander Heller and starring Will Brill (Tony winner for Stereophonic ), Gillian Jacobs and Rob Lowe (who also produces), is out on 250 screens. Convinced he’s a big fish stuck in a small pond, bitter playwright Doug Leibowitz has been marking time as a theater teacher until he can get to New York. But when he finds his ex has been dating the person he hates most in the world, the school principal, his plans shift to secretly staging the most inappropriate play possible at the middle school. Unapologetic Partners, Blue Harbor Entertainment and Variance Films are partnering on the release. Live-action biblical drama Daniel and the Fiery Furnace from EKKL Entertainment arrives on 1,493 screens this weekend. Written and directed by Matthew and Daniel Kooman, it’s the origin story of the prophet Daniel against the backdrop of exile in Babylon. Limited: Watermelon Pictures opens Traces of Home by Colette Ghunim at the Angelika in NYC. The doc follows the filmmaker on a journey of self-discovery as she sets out to reunite her parents with the ancestral homes they were forced to flee as children in Palestine and Mexico. Filmed over five years and featuring animation and archival footage. Executive produced by Melissa Barrera and John Leguizamo. Winner of the Grand Jury Prize in U.S. Competition at DOC NYC last November and Best Documentary Feature at San Diego Latino Film Festival. Expands to Laemmle Royal and Laemmle Glendale in L.A. next week. As Alex Gibney’s Musk makes headlines, the Oscar-winning documentarian has another film out this weekend — Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie opens in 18 theaters via Abramorama. Featuring the writer and his wife Rachel Eliza Griffiths and inspired by Rushdie’s memoir Knife: Meditations After an Attempted Murder , it explores his recovery from a 2022 attack at a speaking engagement where was stabbed 15 times. With personal footage that has never been seen by the public, the doc follows the writer on his physical and spiritual recovery. Quiver Distribution debuts Berlin-premiering coming-of-age drama Sunny Dancer on about 20 screens. A group of teenagers finds friendship at a summer camp for cancer survivors. Stars Bella Ramsey, Neil Patrick Harris, James Norton and Jessica Gunning with a score by Este Haim. In two of the cases, her revenge is fatal. But then she meets the third accomplice, Tito (Demián Bichir), now a clerk in a newspaper kiosk at a train station. Related Stories TIFF Takeaways: A Chris Rock Crowd-Pleaser, Peter Farrelly's 'Rocky' Standing Ovation and Market Growing Pains ‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Review: Takashi Miike’s Loose Remake Is a Complete Nonstarter The movie is in many ways a two-hander featuring Nina and Tito talking over drinks with flashback scenes chronicling both of their sometimes harrowing lives. “I was afraid that I couldn’t play this part, and also I was afraid to go so far every day at work and go into this really difficult place,” Hayek says during a joint interview with Jolie. “At the beginning, I wasn’t sure that Angelina was directing. I thought she was just producing. I’m like, ‘Oh no, I don’t want to suffer like that. I don’t want to.’ And then she started talking to me about the importance of the piece. And then you have to understand that Angelina is an extraordinary director.” Popular on Variety Salma Hayek Pinault stars in “Without Blood.” Courtesy Image “Without Blood” is an adaptation of Italian writer Alessandro Baricco’s novella of the same name. Like the book, the movie doesn’t specify the time or the location where the story takes place, nor identify the war at the center of the story. The characters speak English and Spanish. “I wanted it to be that anyone watching it from anywhere could identify with it,” Jolie says. “Even if it wasn’t an actual war or a conflict, there’s something beautiful in the book where it says, ‘We return to where we break.’ So part of the conflict and the idea of the film is that anybody can identify with something in your life where something happened where it broke you and changed you, and how much you wish you could sit across from that person and have answers and have some kind of say your piece and hope that they could see you and hope that it gives you some kind of healing or closure. Of course, sometimes it doesn’t give you what you think you’re looking for or doesn’t heal those.” This isn’t the first time Jolie has made a film about war and conflict. Her directorial debut was the Bosnian war drama “In the Land of Blood and Money” in 2011. “Unbroken” (2014) told the story of American prisoners-of-war during World War II. The life of Cambodian author and human rights activist Loung Ung under the rule of the Khmer Rouge was the subject of “First They Killed My Father” in 2017. “In ‘First They Killed My Father,’ we had trauma therapy tents because a lot of people there had been through war and I’ve learned that everybody’s been through some level of trauma,” Jolie says. “What we did on this was the time spent with everybody discussing it. We all ended up spending a lot of time talking about our pain, talking about our losses, our traumas. Obviously, community can be very, very healing.” Jolie and Hayek Pinault first worked together five years ago when they co-starred in the Marvel movie “Eternals.” Next, Jolie will serve as a producer on Hayek Pinault’s directorial debut, “Arena,” an epic romantic adventure that the “Frida” star also wrote. “In a way, she’s my partner,” Hayek Pinault says. “I’ve written two different scripts with two different pens that she gave me. It’s a really good, enriching and artistic relationship. That is hard to find. It’s such a gift.” I asked Jolie if she’s ever been tempted to direct lighter material like a comedy. “We’ve laughed a lot. We fantasized about making different comedies together,” Hayek Pinault says. Jolie laughs, “My comedies tend to be a bit dark. I think I have a dark sense of humor.” Hayek Pinault turns to Jolie and says, “You’re funny. So funny. She just keeps it a secret.” Jolie isn’t sure she has what it takes to helm comedy. “I don’t know how good I’d be. You have those things that we think, as an actress, you like to try everything and then you get to a point you realize other actors are good at certain things and there are many who are better at comedy than I am. But I do think I’m a pretty good straight person, like the ‘Maleficent.’ I’m a good straight.” “Without Blood” is in theaters now. title: ‘Sweet Magnolias’ Canceled at Netflix After Five Seasons
full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All September 18, 2026 4:05pm JoAnna Garcia Swisher in season five of 'Sweet Magnolias' Netflix Logo text Netflix has canceled its drama series Sweet Magnolias after five seasons, but its showrunner and one of its lead actresses are also involved in a new show at the streamer. The cancellation of Sweet Magnolias , based on novels by Sherryl Woods, comes three months after season five premiered on Netflix. The show’s audience, both worldwide and in the United States, had fallen off in the fourth and fifth seasons. Season five spent three weeks in Netflix’s worldwide top 10 for English-language series (based on the streamer’s internal data) and four weeks in Nielsen’s U.S. charts. Related Stories Business Netflix Stock Falls After Wells Fargo Downgrade: "Engagement Trends Look Worrying to Us" TV The Eccentric Vicky Krieps on Ryan Murphy, 'Ocean's Eleven,' and Netflix's Pure Punk Lizzie Borden Season of 'Monster' The show stars JoAnna Garcia Swisher, Brooke Elliott and Heather Headley as three long-time best friends who rely on one another through the ups and downs of their lives. As for the new series: Sweet Magnolias showrunner Sheryl J. Anderson and Garcia Swisher are executive producing Ladies of the House , based on a novel by Lauren Edmondson. Garcia Swisher may also have an on-screen role. Ladies of the House centers on a family that owns a winery. When the owner dies unexpectedly, “his wife and two adult daughters must battle through their issues with each other in order to confront challenges with the business, their extended family, and the men in their lives,” the logline reads. Anderson will serve as showrunner and executive produce with Garcia Swisher and Kate Gordon via their Rolling Clover company and Black Label Media. “I’m thrilled to be embarking on this new adventure with JoAnna and Netflix,” said Anderson. “When Jo shared the novel with me, I immediately saw the foundation for a series centered on three women grappling with the complexities of family, friendship, and romance — the kind of stories Jo and I most enjoy telling. I cannot wait to share the Richardson women and their world with Netflix’s global audience.” Added Garcia Swisher, “I am beyond excited to continue to tell meaningful, female-driven stories alongside the incredible Sheryl Anderson, and to bring this to life through our production company, Rolling Clover, and with our wonderful partners at Black Label. Netflix has been my creative home for the past seven years, and I couldn’t imagine a better place, or a better team, to tell this story.” Deadline first reported the cancellation. THR

title: Nick Reiner Pushes for Release of Trust Money to Fund Criminal Trial in New Court Filings
full_text: Skip to main content By Gary Baum Plus Icon Gary Baum Senior Writer garymbaum Follow Sign Up View All September 18, 2026 3:58pm Nick Reiner appears during his arraignment in Los Angeles County Superior Court on Feb. 23, 2026. Chris Torres / AFP via Getty Images Logo text In new civil court filings, lawyers for incarcerated Nick Reiner continue to fight for access to his trust money to pay for his criminal defense as he stands accused of killing his parents, Rob and Michele. Reiner, 32, wants to rehire Alan Jackson, who has represented the likes of Harvey Weinstein and Karen Read. The star attorney previously withdrew from the Los Angeles case for lack of funding. (Prosecutors recently stated they wouldn’t seek the death penalty after consulting Reiner’s siblings.) The trust’s fiduciaries cited a California law known as the “Slayer Statute” as their rationale for not dispersing the money. It prohibits people from receiving an inheritance from those they kill. Reiner’s team has previously argued that the trustees didn’t release a required portion of the funds when he turned 30, before the murders, and their client has yet to be proven guilty of his double-homicide charge. Now, they point out that “a substantial portion” of the disputed funds in the trust — at least $325,000 — is money from his grandfather, Carl Reiner , who died in 2020. “Nick is not accused of causing his death,” the new filing notes. “Money that was left to Nick by his grandfather is not money received by Nick from or through his parents. To the extent the funds Nick received from his grandfather are Nick’s personal assets, they remain Nick’s and should be segregated and released from this trust. Even if they were properly held by the trust, the ‘Slayer Statute’ does not supply a basis for withholding them.” Reiner’s lawyers say that this civil court dispute over nonpayment has so far caused the fiduciaries to pay lawyers more than $250,000 out of his trust to defend themselves. They note that this is itself “nearly half” the size of the age-30 distribution — $558,000 — which Reiner contends he’s overdue. (The trust is valued at $1.6 million.) They’ve told the court that the trustees “have refused to release any money to Nick. He still has not received $1 of his own trust money for basic support and hygiene items while in jail.” Reiner is suing both the now-former fiduciary in charge of his trust, as well as the current one: Jodi Montgomery, who served as Britney Spears’ conservator from 2019 until it was dissolved in 2021 , after Spears’ father was removed from the role.
